He explains the original problem: on launch, the app made about 20 sequential network requests (session, subscription, today's question, XP, leaderboard, etc.), blocking the home screen until all completed — which took 2.8 seconds on fast Wi-Fi and over 30 seconds on slow in-flight Wi-Fi. He details three fixes: 1) Optimistic launch — trusting the locally cached session token to show the home screen immediately at t=0, then validating in the background; 2) Caching a full home-screen snapshot on device using UserDefaults, so zero network requests are needed before first paint; 3) Running remaining network calls in parallel instead of sequentially, reducing total wait time to the slowest single request. He acknowledges trade-offs like slightly stale data, then shows results: cold start dropped from 35 seconds to 3 seconds on slow connections, and to 0.2 seconds after. The tone is educational and enthusiastic, aimed at developers.

transcript: Thus the DaVinci Resolve trick is going to save you heaps of storage and probably heaps of money. I recently finished a commercial project and I ended up with around 166 gigabytes of footage. I didn't want to keep every single rock clip but I also wanted the option to go back and revise the final edits later. So in DaVinci Resolve, go to File, then Media Management, select your timelines, choose Copy and then select Use the media and trim. DaVinci Resolve will only copy the parts of each clip that were actually used in your timelines. You can also add handles which keep a few extra seconds before and after each edit, just in case you need to make changes later. My consolidated archive ended up being around 21 gigabytes. Just make sure you save your project file and test the archive before deleting any of your original footage. I'm still learning this stuff too so if you're figuring out filmmaking as you go, follow along. I'll keep sharing everything I learned.

media_description: A male presenter in a pink shirt and glasses explains a recent Stanford University paper titled 'Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses.' He argues that AI agents are failing not because the underlying LLM is broken, but because developers optimize the wrong component—the 'harness,' which is the code layer that orchestrates tool calls, memory retrieval, and context passing. Using the example of booking a flight, he illustrates how the harness determines success or failure. He contrasts manual hand-tweaking of harnesses by major tech companies with Stanford's Meta-Harness system, which uses a Claude Code Layer to automatically propose, evaluate, and iteratively improve harness code by analyzing logs, failures, and traces. On-screen graphics show performance charts indicating a 6x improvement gap and TerminalBench-2 results where Meta-Harness (37.6) outperformed human-written harnesses like Goose and Terminus-KIRA. The presenter concludes that the harness is becoming as important as the model itself, and teams that automate its optimization will gain a massive advantage. The tone is informative and promotional for the research, posted April 9, 2026.
transcript: Your AI agents are trash because you're optimizing the wrong thing. Stanford dropped the paper a few weeks ago and it basically says your model doesn't matter if your harness is broken. Think about it this way, when you ask an AI agent to, let's say for example, book you a flight, something has to decide when to call the search tool, what to remember, what to pass to the model and what to throw away. That entire orchestration layer, the tool calls, the memory, the retrieval, that's the harness. And depending on how well it's written, the same exact model either crushes the task or completely falls apart. We're talking a six times performance gap on how well your harness layer is. And right now, major tech companies are still building and tweaking these harness layers by hand. But researchers at Stanford introduced the meta harness. Instead of a human engineer sitting down and manually tweaking the harness code, there's a Claude code layer that watches the whole harness. It has access to the code, failure traces and all the logs. So anytime it sees a wrong tool call or some lost context or some bad retrieval from your rag system, it updates and tweaks a part of that code to account for that error. And this repeats so your harness layer is constantly improving better and better. And results were really impressive. On terminal bench two where teams spent weeks hand crafting and fine tuning their harness, meta harness automatically discovered one that beat all of them. A ranked number one amongst all Claude Haiku 4.5 agents. And this points to something bigger. The harness layer is becoming just as important as the model itself. And I think the teams that figure out how to automate and monitor their harness properly, they're going to have a massive advantage over everyone doing it manually. Follow and I'll keep you posted.

media_description: This is a ShotDeck promotional interview featuring senior colorist Sam Daley, known for work on HBO's Succession, The Florida Project, Sorry to Bother You, A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood, and Barbarian. Speaking directly to camera against a pink background, Daley explains his philosophy for grading digital versus film images, using the metaphor that digitally acquired images are like dogs you can play with and dress up, while film is like a cat that needs nurturing. He describes approaching film with a very light touch, citing Succession where he used digital tools sparingly to mimic telecine days for a more natural, filmic feel. He breaks down a favorite shot from The Florida Project, noting it was shot mostly on film but night scenes were captured on Alexa cameras due to lack of night shoot schedules; the production used low ASA film stock for rich colors, resulting in exposures at the bottom of the negative that showcase film's beauty. Daley also discusses grading Barbarian with cinematographer Zach Cooperstein, including a mid-film flashback sequence shot in 4x3 aspect ratio that was approached as if shot on video, deliberately avoiding video idiosyncrasies like scan lines or jitter. He cautions that colorists working on digital images often over-focus on film artifacts such as grain, contrast, halation, and dust, and emphasizes using many tools lightly so no single tool makes the image look obviously digital. The interview is intercut with clips from the referenced films and ends with ShotDeck branding.
transcript: Digitally acquired images are like dogs. You can play with them, you can dress them up, you can groom them, you can teach them tricks. Film is a cat. It's best to just take care of it and nurture it and occasionally it kind of warms up to you. So I approached film with a very light touch. If you look at Succession, I treated it as if I was back in Telus any days. I used digital tools very sparingly so that it would feel more natural and more filmic. Here is one shot. It's one of my favorites from the movie. It was shot on film mostly, but also some of the night scenes were shot on Alexa. They did not have a night shoot schedule so they did not have any digital cameras that Alexa's out. All the film that they had was like low ASA film because they really wanted the rich colors. So the exposure is like really at the bottom of the negative and there's not a lot to get out of it but it really just shows the beauty of film. I graded barbarian with Zach Cooperstein, the cinematographer. There was a moment in the middle of the movie where we break into a flashback and we go four by three. We had to create a whole different look and approached it as if it was shot on video. Avoiding the idiosyncrasy, the format like scan lines or jitter, sometimes with colorists who work on digitally acquired images and try to make them look like film, they're focusing too much on the idiosyncrasies of the format. We're talking grain, contrast, halation, dust. I have a light touch with a lot of different tools so that one tool does not pronounce itself as being digital.

The video opens with shots of the U.S. Capitol at sunset while the creator explains he will show why the Sony FX5's 16-bit X-OCN LT RAW codec outperforms the Sony FX3's 10-bit XAVC S All-Intra codec in under 60 seconds. The scene moves indoors to a studio setup where two identical Sony cameras (FX3 and FX5) on tripods film a table with color charts and a sign. Through three split-screen tests, the creator pushes exposure in post-production: +3 stops from properly exposed, +3 stops from +1 overexposed, and pulling down from +3 overexposed to normal. The results consistently show the FX5 retaining nearly all color information and highlight detail, while the FX3's image becomes faded, blown out, and loses about 50% of information. Close-ups of the sign and color chart emphasize the FX5's superior highlight recovery and color rendition. The creator concludes the FX5 is the clear winner for color grading latitude, though he notes the FX3 still holds up well for being a long-GOP codec. caption:
Viral Dumpling Lasagna 🥟🔥

Comment “Recipe” and I’ll send you the full recipe card for free!!

For ALL of you asking about the app I made, just search “Osta” on the app or play store. It is free & makes cooking social media recipes way easier 🙏

Homemade dumplings meet homemade lasagna 🤝… dare I say easier, quicker, and better than both? 👀

Ingredients: -1 lb (450 g) ground chicken or pork -1/2 cup green onions, chopped -6 garlic cloves, minced -3 tbsp soy sauce -1 tbsp rice vinegar -1 tbsp toasted sesame oil -2 tbsp chili crunch -1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated -1 tbsp oyster sauce -18 to 24 wonton or dumpling wrappers -2 tbsp chicken stock (or water)
For Garnish: -Soy sauce -Chili crunch -Green onions, sliced -Sesame seeds

Instructions:
1. In a bowl, combine the ground chicken or pork with the green onions, garlic, soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, Chili Crunch, ginger, and oyster sauce. Mix with your hands until just combined.
2. Set up a steamer over a pot of gently boiling water. If you don’t have a steamer, simply place a heat-safe rack or trivet inside a large pot instead. Make sure your baking dish fits comfortably inside & the lid can fully close (I used an 8×8-inch dish). Keep the water level below the baking dish.
3. Briefly dip each wrapper in water for just 1–2 secs, then arrange a layer across the bottom of your dish. I used 6 wrappers per layer. Overlap them as needed to completely cover the bottom… the overlap actually helps everything hold together.
4. Spread a thin layer of the meat mixture over the wrappers. Repeat with wrappers and meat until everything is used. I made 4 layers, but work with whatever fits your dish. Finish with a final layer of wrappers, then pour the chicken stock evenly over top.
5. Carefully place the dish into your steamer, cover, & steam for 20–22 mins, keeping the water at a gentle boil. Remove once the meat is cooked through & the top is glossy.
6. Finish with a drizzle of soy sauce, plenty of chili crunch, sliced green onions, and sesame seeds. Slice it up like lasagna and enjoy this new family favorite!

caption:
Chicken alfredo tacos 🌮 

For the chicken:

1 lb boneless chicken breast, cut into small pieces 
Salt to taste
1 tsp black pepper 
1 tsp smoked paprika powder 
1 tbsp garlic powder 
1 tsp onion powder 
1/2 tsp Italian seasoning 
2 tbsp lemon juice 
2 tbsp oil for marinating + more for cooking

For the Alfredo sauce:
2 tbsp butter
1 tbsp all purpose flour 
2 cloves fresh garlic, minced 
1 cup unsweetened heavy whipping cream
Salt to taste 
1/2 tsp black pepper 
1 tsp garlic powder 
1/2 cup milk
3/4 cup Parmesan cheese, freshly grated 

To assemble:
15-16 mini tacos
1 cup mozzarella cheese 
Oil for lightly frying the tacos
1/4 cup parsley, freshly chopped for garnish 

Method 

Marinate the chicken with salt, black pepper, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, Italian seasoning, lemon juice, and oil for 20–30 minutes. Cook until golden and set aside.
In the same pan, melt the butter and sauté the garlic. Whisk in the flour, then add the heavy cream and milk. Season with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Simmer until slightly thickened, then stir in the Parmesan until smooth. 
Add the cooked chicken to half of the sauce and toss to coat. Reserve half for later . Fill each tortilla with mozzarella, the chicken Alfredo mixture, and a little more mozzarella. Fold and pan-fry until golden and crispy on both sides.
Garnish with fresh parsley and serve with extra Alfredo sauce for dipping.

caption:
How to render beef fat into tallow

In an air fryer
150°C (300°F) in three 10-minute bursts. This will leave it very spongy so strain it through a sieve and then use a spoon to press out the remaining oil leaving only the fibre.

In an oven
Set the oven to 110°C to 150°C - some people like a lower temp over the course of several hours, but I've found 150°C speeds things up a bit with no negative effect on the quality of the result.

Put your beef fat or trimmings in a pan and in the oven until rendered down.

On the stove top
As above but on low on a stove top. This can get a bit smelly, but it's a good smell IMO. This will also make the fibre crispy and darker so the taste won't be quite as neutral, especially with trimmings that include little bit of meat.

In a slow-cooker
I've not done this before, but someone suggested it in the comments and it seems like a great way to be able to set it and forget it. I should think you'll end up with a great product too. Note: don't actually forget it.

I'd put the slow cooker on high which is usually 121°C - 149°C.

Why is it called cod fat?

Fair warning, this might put you off a bit!
When a male calf is castrated to become a steer, his testicles are removed. As he grows into a full-sized beef animal, the empty anatomical pocket left behind fills with a dense plug of fat. That fat plug in the steer's pelvic area is cod fat.

And if you’re thinking this sounds suspiciously similar to a knight’s codpiece, you’re spot on. Both terms share the exact same root: the Old English word codd (or Middle English cod), which literally meant "bag," "pouch," or "scrotum."
What to ask your butcher for

"Cod fat" is a bit of an old-school term. Experienced or multi-generational butchers will still know it by name, but if you get a confused look across the counter, just ask for hard suet or pelvic suet.

Thanks to my friend @amylevin_ for putting me on to this.

He explains that the liquid poured over a seared steak is not oil but tallow rendered from £1.89 worth of raw beef fat purchased at a farm shop, claiming it yields seven times more product than a premium store-bought jar. He cuts the fat into small cubes, places them in a glass dish inside the air fryer basket (not directly on the crisper plate to avoid smoking), and cooks at 150°C for three 10-minute cycles, stirring between each. After rendering, he strains the golden liquid through a sieve, presses out remaining fat, and stores the cooled tallow in a glass jar, noting it lasts 12-18 months refrigerated. 1 sheet puff pastry
@smashkitchen organic classic pizza sauce
shredded mozzarella cheese

media_description: In a studio interview on the radio show The Breakfast Club, Texas politician James Talarico speaks into a microphone while seated across from the show's hosts, including a man in a New York Yankees cap and a woman host. He argues that Texas' ban on THC products is not about public health but about corruption, stating that industries most worried about THC being readily available are Big Beer and Big Tobacco, which he says pushed the ban because it hurts their bottom line. He cites research that THC and cannabis products are safer and less addictive than beer or tobacco, calling the situation a prime example of big industries buying politicians to push bills that harm people but benefit them financially. Talarico notes that many young Texans and veterans use THC products for PTSD, and that Texas legalized hemp six years ago, creating a booming industry of local small businesses. He contends the ban is a gift to drug cartels because Texans will continue to use cannabis but will now buy it on the black market instead of from regulated local shops, driving people to unknown products. He expresses frustration that policies actively hurt people who are struggling to afford basics, and concludes that government should make lives easier, not harder. The hosts react, with one joking about the "burning bush" in the Bible, to which Talarico responds that hemp was legalized recently.

caption:
Garlic parmesan cheeseburger bombs 🍔 

For all of you asking - the app link for Osta is in my bio or you can search “Osta Recipes” on the App Store or Google Play store! 💕 Save this recipe and thank me later ;)

RECIPE ⬇️
* 1 lb 80/20 ground beef
* 1 tsp garlic powder
* 1 tsp onion powder 
* 2 tsp Worcestershire 
* Minced garlic 
* Salt & pepper to taste 
* Optional add-ins: caramelized onions, bacon
* Mild cheddar, large cubes
* Shredded mozzarella 
* 1 can biscuit dough (Pillsbury original flakey layers)
* 1 egg, whisked (for egg wash)
* Parmesan 

Garlic butter:
* 3 tbs salted butter, melted
* 2 cloves garlic, finely minced
* Dried or fresh parsley

1. Cook the ground beef on medium heat. Once browned, add minced garlic and all the seasonings. Stir for a minute. Set aside. 
2. Preheat oven to 375F
3. Take each biscuit and stretch it into a 5 inch circle. Add 2 spoonfuls of seasoned beef, some mozzarella, and a cube of cheese in the middle. 
4. Fold the dough around the filling and pinch the edges tightly to seal. Pull it into a tight ball. Rest 5 min.
5. Place them seam side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush a thin layer of egg wash and sprinkle fresh grated parmesan.
6. Bake at 375F for 15-18 min until deeply golden.
7. Brush on garlic butter and sprinkle more parmesan. Serve immediately.

#cheeseburgers #garlicparmesan #garlicknots #dinneridea #cheapmeals

author: jasonkpargin
media_description: A man, identified as author Jason Pargin, discusses the famously viral daily writing schedule of James Bond creator Ian Fleming. He reads the schedule aloud while it is displayed on screen: wake at 7:30am, bathe in the ocean, breakfast, write 1,500 words from 10am to 12:15pm without editing, snorkel for lobsters, lunch with pink gins, nap, garden and swim, write another 500 words at 5pm, dinner and Scrabble with his wife Ann, bed at 10pm. Pargin explains this occurred at Fleming's vacation home in Jamaica, called Goldeneye, overlooking the beach. He notes Fleming wrote about 2,000 words per day, finished a first draft in roughly six weeks, then spent a week revising before sending it to the publisher. Pargin contrasts this with his own much less famous series, which took about two years per book. He points out the irony that while the schedule sounds stress-free and ideal for longevity, Fleming died of a heart attack at age 56. He adds that the schedule keeps going viral because it came from Fleming's final Playboy interview, and despite Fleming's relatively short life, he made the most of it.

caption: I’m 100% against Flock, but there’s definitely something fishy going on… 🤔
media_description: In a July 2026 video, independent journalist James Li (@5149jamesli) addresses viral clips of people destroying Flock Safety license-plate cameras across the U.S. He opens by saying the trend looks "super badass" but then questions whether the sudden explosion in anti-Flock coverage is organic or a coordinated effort. Using Google Trends data, news clips from Denver, and articles from The Denver Post, CNBC, and KTAR News, he argues that while Denver publicly parted ways with Flock after public outcry, the city instead awarded millions to Axon Enterprise — the multi-billion-dollar company behind Tasers, police body cameras, and AI crime centers. He notes Axon's aggressive lobbying and cites reporting that President Donald Trump personally invested up to $5 million in Axon stock, suggesting a financial interest in expanding privatized law-enforcement infrastructure. Li concludes by asking whether the viral backlash against Flock is inadvertently clearing the way for an even larger, better-connected defense-tech monopoly to take over America's mass surveillance ambitions, framing it as a question rather than a definitive claim.

author: noaa.very
caption:
Student loan forgiveness isn't about spending new taxpayer dollars—it's about wiping away fabricated debt created by runaway interest. Think of it like this: if you borrow $100 and accrue $300 in interest over time, you now owe $400. If the lender forgives $100 of that accumulated balance, they aren't out-of-pocket for a single new dollar. They are simply erasing interest that only ever existed on paper.
This image perfectly breaks down the misconception surrounding student loan relief programs. Opponents often claim that forgiveness is a massive expense funded directly by working-class taxes. In reality, the vast majority of debt slated for relief consists of capitalized interest—fees that stacked up long after the initial principle loan was distributed. The government isn’t cutting new checks to borrowers; it is adjusting an inflated ledger.
Understanding how the system works changes the entire conversation around economic relief. Forgiving this debt doesn't cost the public money; it simply stops penalizing people for predatory interest structures. It’s time to stop treating bookkeeping corrections like government spending.
#StudentLoanForgiveness #DebtRelief #StudentLoans #EconomicJustice #financialliteracycampaign

caption: The trick to moist, tender ground beef? A sprinkle of baking soda. @gitsini shares the science behind why it works and the proof that will make you a believer.
media_description: A male presenter demonstrates a cooking hack titled 'Why Baking Soda Makes Better Ground Beef.' He explains that adding baking soda — a technique borrowed from classic Chinese stir-fry recipes — makes any ground meat more tender and juicy. The video shows him retrieving an Arm & Hammer box of pure baking soda, then mixing 1/4 teaspoon of it with 1 tablespoon of water and incorporating it into one pound of raw ground beef. He advises letting the mixture sit for 15 minutes for full benefit, though it starts working in five. Animated diagrams illustrate the science: baking soda raises the meat's pH, causing muscle fibers to repel each other so they can't squeeze out moisture during cooking, resulting in a juicier texture; the higher pH also promotes better browning through the Maillard reaction. A side-by-side comparison shows treated beef browning darker than untreated. The presenter notes the trick works for ground beef, turkey burgers, pork meatballs, shepherd's pie, and stir-fries. The video concludes with plated examples, including lettuce wraps topped with the cooked beef, cucumber, and sauce.
transcript: There is a quick trick to make any ground meat recipe more tender and more juicy and it's probably in your cabinet right now. Just add baking soda. This is a trick inspired by technique in many classic Chinese stir fry recipes. Baking soda raises the pH of the meat which alters the charge on the muscle filaments so that they repel each other. As a result they can't contract as easily and squeeze out their water so the meat is going to hold onto moisture better which makes it more tender and juicy. But that's not all baking soda brings to the table. A higher pH also means better browning because the mild reaction favors an alkaline environment. Check out this batch of ground beef that I treated with baking soda versus this untreated one. So this one just has a quarter teaspoon of baking soda added to a tablespoon of water that I incorporated into a pound of meat. Combining it with the water helps you to distribute it more evenly. For the full benefit let the mixture sit for 15 minutes but it'll start working as soon as five then you can continue your recipe as normal. We've done this trick with ground beef chili, turkey burgers, pork meatballs, shepherd's pie and a load of stir fries. It's just one easy step that really makes a delicious difference.

caption:
The SFPD’s exposure of hours of videos from drone platform Skydio reveals how broadly it’s watching the city from above—and how the results can spill online.

Tap the 🔗 in bio for the full story.
media_description: A WIRED video hosted by Andy Greenberg reports on leaked San Francisco Police Department drone footage. Security researchers Sam Curry and Mike Robert discovered that Skydio's platform was publicly livestreaming real-time color and thermal video from five SFPD quadcopters on the open web. They reported the leak to Skydio; the link was removed after about three hours, but they had already saved roughly three hours of video from two days of flights. The footage shows police operations including officers surrounding and tackling a man in a parking lot viewed from multiple drones, officers dismounting scooters to detain someone, and views inside an apartment courtyard. In one "prowler" incident, a drone zooms on a young person wearing headphones on a rooftop, unaware. In another, a drone follows a car suspected of theft for ten minutes until occupants exit and play basketball. The SFPD called the stream an internal restricted link improperly accessed; the researchers said no hack was used, and someone with access created an unauthenticated link in December with a one-year expiration. Analysis of the 20 recordings shows hundreds of people and vehicles filmed, with dozens of faces visible, despite SFPD policy to minimize recording uninvolved people. No subjects look up at the drones, suggesting their small size and altitude make them virtually invisible. The video directs viewers to wired.com for the full story.

author: pulseusa2
caption:
This lecture, delivered in an undisclosed U.S. city, features Nobel laureate Milton Friedman discussing the historical paradox of immigration policy in the United States. 

Friedman reflects on the era of completely free immigration prior to 1914, noting that while almost everyone viewed it as a net positive then, the same policy is rejected today. 

This clip is directly related to current Republican and conservative discourse regarding immigration reform, border security, and the imperative to protect the American labor market from undue strain.

Friedman argues that while free immigration to seek jobs benefits all parties, the introduction of a pervasive welfare state creates a significant barrier to such open policies. He asserts that a nation cannot realistically maintain both unlimited immigration and a system where every resident is guaranteed a certain level of income or subsistence, regardless of employment status.

This aligns with conservative perspectives that prioritize fiscal responsibility and emphasize that robust welfare systems must be balanced with strict, merit-based immigration controls to avoid eroding the economy.

The final segment highlights Friedman's assertion that the presence of social safety nets forces a necessary reconsideration of immigration. He suggests that the perception of these potential economic consequences—where unchecked immigration could lead to a reduction in the standard of living for current residents—is what drives the shift from historical support to modern skepticism of open borders. 

This line of reasoning is a cornerstone of the contemporary Republican platform, which consistently ties the necessity for strong border enforcement to the preservation of national sovereignty and the stability of American social and economic welfare.

#ConservativeEconomics #BorderSecurity #FiscalResponsibility #EconomicLiberty #USPolicy
media_description: The video shows archival footage of Nobel Prize-winning economist Milton Friedman speaking at a podium. On-screen text identifies him and the topic as 'Illegal Immigration,' with a small U.S. flag graphic. Friedman, wearing a dark suit and glasses, delivers a measured lecture explaining what he calls a paradox: before 1914, the United States had effectively free immigration, and nearly everyone agreed it was beneficial. Today, the same idea is widely rejected. He argues the difference is not immigration itself, but the existence of a welfare state. Free immigration to jobs, where newcomers come to work and mutually benefit existing residents and themselves, is viable. However, free immigration to welfare — where every resident is promised a minimum level of income regardless of work — is not sustainable, because it creates a perception that more people sharing the pot will reduce everyone's share. He notes this perception, even if exaggerated, drives people to adopt seemingly inconsistent positions on immigration. The clip is presented with a caption linking Friedman's argument to contemporary Republican and conservative discourse on border security, fiscal responsibility, and limiting immigration due to welfare costs.

caption:
Cinnamon rolls… made in 20 minutes, and every bite is the center of the cinnamon Roll

In depth recipe with pictures on substack!!!

🛒 Ingredients

Dough

1 cup (130g) all purpose flour
1 tsp baking powder
1/4 tsp salt
1 tsp cinnamon
1/3 cup (80ml) milk (or half milk, half heavy cream)
1 tsp vanilla
1 tbsp melted butter

Coating

1 tbsp melted butter
3 tbsp sugar
1-2 Tsp cinnamon

Vanilla Bean Glaze ✨

4 tbsp powdered sugar
2 tsp heavy cream
1/2 tsp vanilla
Vanilla bean or vanilla bean paste
👨‍🍳 Instructions

1️⃣ Preheat oven to 375°F and grease or line your pan

2️⃣ In a bowl, whisk together flour, baking powder, salt, and cinnamon

3️⃣ Warm milk slightly, then mix in vanilla and melted butter

4️⃣ Pour wet into dry and mix until a soft dough forms, stop as soon as it comes together, don’t overmix

5️⃣ Lightly flour your surface, roll dough into a log, flatten slightly, and cut into 20 even bites

6️⃣ Toss each piece in melted butter, then coat fully in cinnamon sugar

7️⃣ Place in pan in a single layer with a little space between each, no stacking

8️⃣ Bake 9 to 10 minutes, until lightly golden, don’t overbake

9️⃣ While baking, mix glaze until smooth, adjust thickness if needed

🔟 Let bites cool 1 to 2 minutes, drizzle glaze over the top while warm, and enjoy

⏱ Time & Servings
Prep 10 min
Cook 10 min
Serves 2 to 3
🔥 Pro Tip

Mix just until the dough comes together, overmixing is what makes these dense instead of soft and pillowy.

Hope yall love these, tag me if you make them!!

#cinnamonroll #cooking #instagood #cinnamonbread #baking

Taylor said the cuts removed the heart and motivations, calling the final product vulgar. The presenter concludes the film isn't great, but the entrance scene remains unforgettable and hard to top even with today's CGI.

author: evolving.ai
caption:
🇮🇳🤖 Some of the most valuable data in robotics is being recorded in ordinary kitchens in southern India.

Workers there, many of them housewives, strap smartphones to their foreheads and film themselves doing chores like slicing mangoes and folding clothes.

The footage is shot in first person, capturing exactly what their hands see, which is the viewpoint a humanoid robot needs to learn from.

One worker in Chennai earns about 250 rupees an hour, close to $2.6. Indian data firms like Objectways process the clips and tag every movement, while US companies such as Micro1 gather more than 160,000 hours of footage a month and still call it far short of what they need.

The demand comes from Tesla, Figure AI, and others racing to build humanoids while real-world data stays scarce.

Robots used to be programmed motion by motion. Now they learn by copying recorded human demonstrations, which is why everyday household behavior has quietly become one of the most sought after materials in the robotics industry.

author: wired
caption:
It’s like “Big Brother” without any limits, or broadcast standards. WIRED goes on location—and on camera—with the cult hit “Fishtank Live.”

📸 Mark Peterson/ Redux Pictures @markpetersonpixs

Tap the 🔗 in bio for the full story.
media_description: The video is a split-screen explainer from WIRED reporter Owen Long describing 'Fishtank Live,' billed as the most extreme reality show you've never heard of. While he speaks to camera, the top half shows footage of ten young contestants called 'fish' living under constant surveillance in a suburban house rigged with dozens of CCTV cameras, mics and speakers. Producers run the show from the basement, using upstairs monitors to host unsettling elimination challenges until one winner takes $50,000. Visuals show contestants strapped with yellow sticky traps covered in crickets, a boxing match where one man strikes another on the ground, and people in distress. Long explains that unmoderated, often hateful messages paid for by viewers are blasted through speakers like a live comments section. He notes the show is broadcast 24/7 online, has been kicked off Twitch and YouTube, now streams on its own site, and has drawn attention from figures like Joe Rogan and Bam Margera. His personal experience inside the house includes seeing custom meme TVs, watching contestants roll in insects, and witnessing a mild-mannered contestant suddenly attack another fish, which he describes as feeling like 'our own personal hell.'
transcript: The most extreme reality show you've probably never heard of is Fish Tank Live. In fact, describing it as a reality show hardly does it justice. And I'm speaking from personal experience as the first journalist to be allowed into the show itself. Let me explain. Fish Tank Live features real people living in a house being filmed, but that's where the comparisons with Big Brother or the real world end. This is much stranger and much darker. It takes place in a suburban home rigged with dozens of CCTV cameras, mics, and speakers. Each season, 10 contestants or fish move in. They face increasingly unsettling elimination challenges until the last one standing wins $50,000. The producers who run the show live in the basement and come upstairs to host challenges, cause chaos and occasionally strap-on boxing gloves to pummel contestants physically, as well as metaphorically. Unsensitive messages, featuring obscenities, slurs, and insults sent in by paying viewers blare through speakers in each room, like an unmoderated comment section sprung to life. As the days and weeks go on, the initially quite shy contestants, most of young people, unemployed and no longer in school, strip naked fight, run directly into plate-glass doors, and do much worse things that I can't say here without this video being moderated. All this is broadcast live online and runs 24-7 for 6 weeks straight. It's quite simply the most extreme reality show in history. It's already been drummed out of 4 neighborhoods in 3 states for violating zoning laws after facing moderation issues with Twitch and YouTube. It now streams on its own website and kick. And if all this sounds fringe, Fish Tank Live is moving closer to the mainstream with each passing day. Organizing say it's making millions on a tiny budget, boosted by corporate sponsors as well as paying fans. It's drawn the attention of Joe Rogan and Bam Margera of Jackass is now a host. I got a slice of what it feels like to be a fish when I stepped inside the Fish Tank myself. Within hours, I'd spoken to twin sisters who introduced themselves as Bingo and Bongo and weren't sure what day it was. I saw a TV that plays only custom memes sent in by fans, and watched as contestants rolled around on the ground while trying to pick up as many dead crickets as possible. I also witnessed what I thought was a mild matter of contestant attacking another fish and a boxing belt. His eyes suddenly filled with hate. As another contestant told me, welcome to our own personal hell. Read the full story of Wired.com.

author: 2xidoo
caption:
@novig | The 2026 NBA Finals ended on a moment of pure defensive collapse that will haunt San Antonio fans for years. Exclusive sideline footage reveals the exact second the Spurs defensive scheme disintegrated during the final seconds of the deciding game. As the Knicks rotated their lineup following a timeout, the Spurs players on the floor including Harper, Vassell, Castle, and Wemby appeared visibly lost. You can clearly see them darting their eyes and pointing frantically while attempting to decipher their new assignments. This critical moment of miscommunication pulled Wemby away from the paint where he was most needed. That single lapse in coverage left OG Anunoby completely unguarded right under the basket, allowing him to secure the game winning tip in that effectively sealed the championship for New York. It is a painful reminder that even the most elite teams can crumble when composure fades during the highest pressure moments of a title series.

—

Beyond the frantic defensive breakdown, deeper analysis of the final possession reveals a much more controversial officiating blunder that went completely unpunished. Before the final shot occurred, Karl Anthony Towns delivered a clear, uncalled elbow directly to Wemby while fighting for position in the paint. This contact forced the star center off balance, which directly contributed to the space required for the winning bucket. While the defensive confusion was the primary catalyst for the defeat, this missed call highlights the thin margin between victory and heartbreak. Losing a championship this way is a devastating conclusion to an incredible season.

#NBAFinals #Spurs #Knicks #Basketball
media_description: The video presents overhead broadcast footage from Madison Square Garden during the 2026 NBA Finals, focusing on the final seconds after a San Antonio timeout. White text at the top frames it as "unreleased footage" showing the Spurs in "utter confusion." The narration emphasizes that Wemby ends up far above the three-point line instead of protecting the rim, leaving OG Anunoby completely unguarded under the basket. The play unfolds with Jalen Brunson taking a contested three-pointer, Wemby getting a fingertip on it, and OG tipping the ball in for the win. On-screen captions and the creator's written caption reinforce the claim that this miscommunication cost San Antonio the championship, and add a disputed claim that KAT delivered an uncalled elbow to Wemby before the shot. caption:
The 14-Day Bikini: How a Small Beach Town Hijacked Fast Fashion

How does a TikTok trend become a finished product in your shopping cart in just 14 days? It’s not a giant mega-factory. We traced 25% of the world's swimwear back to a decentralized "Hive Network" of living-room workshops in Huludao, China. Discover the "Small Order, Quick Return" matrix that makes SHEIN and fast-fashion possible. 

The ultimate lesson in agile manufacturing is speed. Breaking down the decentralized "Hive Network" of Huludao, and how family workshops dominate the global swimwear market. Why traditional apparel brands are dying under inventory costs, and how you can plug into the ecosystem.
#ericonchina #ericsourcing #globaltrade #sourcingexpert #sourcingagent #chinasourcing #sourcingchina #sourcingtips #buyerinsights #supplychain #globalbusiness #manufacturing #fastfashion #dtcbrands #sheinofficial #swimwearfashion #apparelsourcing #fashionindustry
media_description:
The video opens with a title card 'The 14-Day Bikini: How a Small Beach Town Hijacked Fast Fashion' and a split-screen showing a fashion influencer in a neon pink and green bikini on TikTok in Miami, contrasted with the speaker, a man in a blue polo shirt and glasses, in an office setting. He explains that exactly 14 days after the influencer wears the new style, an identical $15 bikini appears in shopping carts. He dismantles the Western assumption of a dystopian mega-factory with 10,000 workers, stating as a supply-chain expert that such a factory does not exist.

He traces the production to Huludao, a freezing beach town in northeastern China, where Chinese supply chains abandoned the traditional mega-factory model because it is too slow to retool. Instead, Huludao built a decentralized 'hive' of thousands of micro-workshops operating in living rooms, with families running five or six high-speed sewing machines surrounded by rolls of spandex. This system executes 'Small Order Quick Return': brands order 500 units, not 100,000, with fabric and elastic suppliers located down the street or next door. A workshop can download a design and produce a test batch in three days; if it goes viral, a central network pings 50 neighboring family workshops to scale to 50,000 units without building a new factory.

The speaker argues this makes inventory a liability and speed the only asset, declaring brands that order six months in advance 'already dead.' The video intercuts his narration with footage of colorful bikinis on racks, close-ups of hands sewing floral and leopard-print fabric on JUKI and ZOJE machines, aerial views of Huludao's cityscape, and shots of fabric cutting tables. It concludes with a direct call to action to subscribe and visit his sourcing website, globalseraph.com, for a buyer office in China.

author: ginny_clarke
caption:
The word "meritocracy" was invented in 1958 as a warning. British sociologist Michael Young wrote a satirical novel imagining a future where society was organized entirely by measured merit. In his dystopia, the "talented" lorded their success over everyone else, convinced their position was deserved because the system said so. It was dark comedy. 

A cautionary tale.

By the 1960s, politicians and business leaders were using it as a positive ideal. In 2001, shortly before he died, Young wrote a piece expressing horror that his satirical term had been adopted as a goal. The thing he created to mock had become the thing everyone wanted.

We've been building systems around a word its own author spent his final years trying to take back. Full video on YT.
media_description: The video is a single-shot interview-style clip featuring Ginny Clarke, identified on screen as a Conscious Leadership Expert. She sits in a well-lit indoor setting wearing a rust-colored polo shirt, large black glasses, gold hoop earrings, and a gold bracelet, speaking directly to camera. On-screen text introduces the topic as 'The Meritocracy Myth.' Clarke explains that the term meritocracy was never meant to be a good thing, noting it was invented in 1958 when Michael Young published a satirical dystopian novel called The Rise of Meritocracy. She describes Young's imagined future where society was organized entirely by measured merit through IQ tests and assessments, which led to a rigid class system where the talented lorded their success over the untalented, believing their position deserved because it was based on objective measures. She calls the book satire, dark comedy, and a cautionary tale about confusing measurement with human worth. Clarke then notes the tragic irony that by the 1960s politicians and business leaders were using meritocracy as a positive ideal, and in 2001 shortly before he died, Young wrote expressing horror at how his satirical term had been adopted as a goal. She closes by offering viewers tools she has developed, mentioning a career map, a community called Awakened Path, and a masterclass on perfectionism coming soon, asking them to comment 'AWAKEN' to receive them.

author: michellcclark
author_name: Michell C. Clark | author, speaker, artist
caption:
There’s a specific kind of grief that comes from seeing people you love suffer directly and indirectly from the consequences of a public safety approach that stopped working a long time ago.

For decades, we were told the answer was more police, more prisons, more time. And the cities that leaned hardest into it kept burying the most people.

What’s happening in Baltimore doesn’t have to be an exception to the rule. It can be a new norm across our nation, if leaders decide to focus on what’s actually been proven to work.

What Baltimore did: identified the small group of people most at risk of shooting or being shot, made them a real offer of help, and made clear there would be consequences if they chose to cause harm anyway.

Police, clergy, hospitals, schools, and violence interrupters all coordinated. They call it Group Violence Reduction. Last year, it helped drive Baltimore’s homicide count to a 50-year low.

Boston, Philly, Detroit, and Indianapolis are running versions of the same playbook and seeing historic drops in violence. 

D.C. is less than 40 miles from Baltimore. We already have violence interrupters doing real work here in D.C. What we don’t have is coordination.

Let’s educate ourselves and the people around us so that we can use our voices constructively.

Comment “conversation” and I’ll message you with a guide that equips you to have authentic, impactful conversations with people you love about what actually makes cities safer.

author: movifyme
caption:
One of the coolest behind-the-scenes secrets of the 2026 Lord of the Flies series is how they filmed the night scenes. Since the show stars young child actors, they are not allowed to work during actual nighttime hours, so the filmmakers had a big problem: how do you make something look dark and scary when you are filming in the middle of the day? Their solution was to use infrared cameras. These are special cameras that work differently from normal cameras, instead of capturing the light that our eyes can see, they capture a type of invisible light called infrared light, which is constantly bouncing off everything around us without us ever noticing it. When you film using infrared, the world looks completely different, trees and leaves that are normally green turn bright white or glowing pink, skies turn deep and moody, and everything gets a strange, almost magical look to it. In this series, the tropical island jungle ended up glowing in beautiful but unsettling shades of neon pink and orange, making it look like no real place on Earth. What was originally just a practical solution to protect the young cast from late night shoots accidentally became one of the most visually striking creative decisions in the whole series. The island ended up feeling creepy, dreamlike and dangerous, which is exactly the kind of mood the story needed. Sometimes the best ideas come from solving the simplest problems.

Lord of the Flies (2026)

media_description: This is a biomechanics instructional video by Conor Harris (@conor_harris_) posted March 3, 2026, explaining how to properly perform a dead hang from a bar to maximize shoulder and chest opening. The video alternates between the instructor demonstrating the hang in a gym setting and 3D anatomical animations showing muscles (latissimus dorsi, pecs) and skeleton mechanics. He explains that most people hang with an arched lower back, which shortens the spine and only stretches the upper fibers of the lats attached to the arm bone. The correct method involves elevating feet on a bench to achieve slight relative spinal flexion/rounding at the lower back while maintaining length through the upper spine, allowing maximal stretch through all lat attachment points. He emphasizes adding breath work—inhaling to expand the ribcage and exhaling to relax—to improve rib mobility, since a compressed ribcage limits the stretch. Key cues: set bar height so pelvis is level with ground, keep neck and traps relaxed, hold softly for 5-10 seconds, breathe gently through nose, and feel side abs/obliques engage and chest/lats open further on exhale.

caption:
Dumpling Lasagna 🥟 

Comment “Recipe” and I’ll send you the full recipe for free.

This dumpling lasagna is actually worth the hype. It’s simple, fun to put together, and easily one of my favorite ways to switch up dumplings.

If you’re tired of eating the same boring meals every week, this is exactly why I share Weeknight Staples.

Follow for more ways to eat better and spend less.

Ingredients
• 1 lb ground pork
• 1/3 cup green onions, thinly sliced
• 1 tbsp fresh ginger, grated
• 4 garlic cloves, minced
• 1 tbsp oyster sauce
• 1 tsp pepper
• 2 tbsp chili crisp
• 3 tbsp soy sauce
• 1½ tsp sesame oil
• 1 tbsp rice vinegar
• Dumpling wrappers (20–25)
• 1/4 cup chicken broth

For topping
• Soy sauce
• Chili crisp
• Green onions
• Sesame seeds

Instructions
1.	In a bowl, mix together the ground pork, green onions, ginger, garlic, oyster sauce, chili crisp, pepper, soy sauce, sesame oil, and rice vinegar until well combined.
2.	Lightly dip each dumpling wrapper in water, then start layering in a baking dish. Begin with wrappers, add a layer of pork, and repeat until everything is used.
3.	Pour the chicken broth evenly across the top.
4.	Cook using one of these methods:
	•	Steam: Bring water to a boil in a large pot, place the dish inside, cover, and steam for 20–23 minutes until cooked through.
	•	Oven: Set the dish inside a larger pan filled with hot water, cover tightly with foil, and bake at 375°F for 30–35 minutes.
5.	Finish with soy sauce, chili crisp, green onions, and sesame seeds before serving.

caption:
Korean Popcorn Chicken 🍗

Comment “Recipe” and I’ll send you the full recipe for free.

If you’re always looking for new dinner ideas, you’re in the right place. That’s why I share simple and affordable meals that help you eat better and spend less.

Follow me for more weeknight staples.

Ingredients

Chicken
• 2 lb chicken breast (or thighs), cut into bite-size pieces
• 2 eggs
• 3 tbsp soy sauce
• ¾ tsp salt
• ¾ tsp black pepper
• 1½ tsp garlic powder
• 1 tsp ginger powder

Crispy Coating
• 1 cup cornstarch
• 3 tbsp flour
• ¾ tsp baking powder

Korean Sauce
• ⅓ cup gochujang
• 3 tbsp brown sugar
• 3 tbsp ketchup
• 4 tbsp honey
• 3 cloves garlic, minced
• 3 tbsp soy sauce
• 3 tbsp rice vinegar
• 1½ tbsp sesame oil
• 1 tbsp butter

Garnish
• green onions
• sesame seeds

Instructions
1.	In a large bowl, combine the chicken, eggs, soy sauce, salt, pepper, garlic powder, and ginger powder. Mix until the chicken is fully coated.
2.	Add the cornstarch, flour, and baking powder. Toss until the chicken is evenly coated.
3.	Cook the chicken.
Air fryer: Preheat to 400°F. Cook for 8 minutes, flip the chicken, then cook another 4 minutes until crispy.
Oven: Bake at 425°F for 15–20 minutes, flipping halfway through.
4.	In a pan over medium heat, combine the gochujang, brown sugar, ketchup, honey, garlic, soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sesame oil. Let it simmer for 3–4 minutes until thick, then turn off the heat and whisk in the butter.
5.	Add the crispy chicken to a bowl and pour in about ½ cup of the sauce. Toss until fully coated, adding more sauce if needed.
6.	Serve over rice and top with green onions and sesame seeds.

It stars Jesse Buckley, Christian Bale, Peter Sarsgaard, Penelope Cruz, and Annette Benning, and it is a lot. A bubbling-over postmodern stew of carloff monsters, classic musicals, film noir, and even a dash of Mel Brooks. And at times, it's delightfully campy, thrillingly energetic, and utterly captivating. It's undeniable that Gyllenhaal had a vision, and she really went for it 172%. As did her collaborators, and you can tell most of the cast and crew went on that journey with her. Jesse Buckley gives a powerful, full-throated dual performance, dipping in and out of different accents. It's really wild, but always fascinating, and the technical filmmaking is rich with bold cinematography and contrasted lighting. The movie really comes alive in its experimental moments and fast-paced action set pieces. The production design is evocative and super stylized throughout. There's a lot of really beautiful-looking urban location shooting, and complex scenes with a ton of background actors. We also got some gnarly and striking makeup effects, and I appreciated that it was occasionally funny. It was a relief to know that Gyllenhaal has a sly sense of humor about all this. For example, there's a winking cameo from her brother Jake that really works. As for Maggie Gyllenhaal's writing, I was compelled by her meta-textual desire to reclaim Shelly's autonomy as Shelly in the story is trying to reclaim the bride's autonomy. Now that said, flipping to the negatives here, the themes are so overt, sometimes the characters speak them literally in the dialogue that it becomes overwhelming and at times off-putting. And then the tone really is a big issue, because the campiness and the outrageousness sits on such a knife's edge, and sometimes it tips too far over into just being corny. But then there are moments with the opposite problem where it's too serious. Mostly during Sarasgard and Cruz's scenes, the movie grinds to a halt for some very solemn, grounded, and frankly lifeless conversations. Which at times had me wondering, what is this supposed to be? Is it a cartoon or not? Which then makes it a bit hard to buy into the world, because the inconsistent ways the characters are reacting to what's happening. And an Epennings character is supremely underwritten and her performance felt way too modern like she's in some other movie. Additionally, the plot momentum and pacing in the editing was very inconsistent. Maggie Gyllenhaal couldn't keep hold of the tension at crucial moments. But here's the thing, I was never bored. The bride was never not watchable, because Gyllenhaal had a vision and she made choices to execute it, even if they weren't always successful. So shout out to Warner Brothers for giving her a big budget to take that big swing. We need more bold movies like this, not less.

author: surajpatelnyc
caption:
If you’re older than 25, you’re older than ICE.
And that’s precisely why refusing to abolish it is actually the extreme position.
For most of American history, we did not have immigration enforcement as we know it today. From roughly 1800 to 1924, the United States operated with what was effectively an open-border system. There were no visas, no green cards, no deportation force. If you arrived, you were generally allowed to stay — and in time, you became American.
Then came a familiar chain of events.
A global Spanish Flu pandemic swept the world in 1918. Supply chains were snarled. Inflation surged. Economic anxiety spread. And political leaders, facing fear and instability, went looking for someone to blame.
Inflation rises. Housing tightens. Supply chains strain. And once more, immigrants are blamed for economic forces they did not cause. Fear hardens into grievance. Scarcity becomes political currency. And the instinctive response is to close off rather than invest forward.
The scapegoat was immigrants. Isolationism surged and America elected the most scandal-plagued president in its history — well, until now. 
So, in 1924, Congress passed the Immigration Act — effectively shutting down immigration through national-origin quotas designed explicitly to preserve the country’s existing ethnic makeup. In fact, so awful was this law that the drafters wrote its racism into the Congressional Record: “The purpose of this act is to preserve the ideal of U.S. homogeneity.” It’s radical, it’s disgusting, and frankly it’s Stephen Miller and Donald Trump’s explicit position. They consider it an intellectual underpinning but really, it’s just simply racist. 
After 1924, legal immigration collapsed almost overnight. Paired with tariffs and protectionism, those policies did not protect American workers. They deepened and prolonged the Great Depression, destabilized democracies abroad, and helped create the political conditions that ultimately led to World War II.
If that story feels eerily familiar, it should. And we are living through the same dumb mistakes again. 
Closed borders did not save the economy. They helped break it.
[cont. in comments]
media_description: A man stands in front of a blackboard, delivering a passionate and informative monologue about the history of US immigration policy. He argues that the creation of ICE in 2001 was a mistake, and that the organization should be abolished. He uses a timeline on the blackboard to illustrate his points, showing how US immigration policy has evolved from open borders in the 1800s, to closed borders in the 1920s, to a more open policy in 1964, and finally to the current system under ICE. He traces the creation of ICE back to the national security apparatus created after 9/11, arguing that it has moved immigration enforcement away from the justice system and into a realm of national security. He concludes by urging viewers to contact their senators to vote against funding ICE.

author: songss
caption:
Just a Friend became iconic by doing the opposite of what hip-hop usually aimed for.

Released in 1989, the song stood out because Biz Markie leaned fully into humor, vulnerability, and intentionally off-key singing. The chorus wasn’t polished or melodic — and that was the point. It made the story feel real, awkward, and relatable.

Built around a sample of Freddie Scott’s “(You) Got What I Need,” the track told a simple heartbreak story almost everyone recognizes: thinking you’re more than friends… and finding out you’re not. Its honesty, comedy, and self-awareness helped push hip-hop into more personal and expressive territory at a time when bravado dominated the genre.

Decades later, Just a Friend still resonates — not because it’s perfect, but because it’s human.

#BizMarkie #HipHopHistory #ClassicHipHop #MusicHistory #JustAFriend

After the New York City mayoral race was called for Zohran Mamdani the night of November 4, the mothers of the Upper East Side began to panic.

“Shocked,” one Facebook user wrote anonymously in the Moms of the Upper East Side (MUES) group, which has 35,000 members. “With all my love for NYC I can’t believe 50% +- of the city voted for this joker. Wondering who’s actually leaving?” Residents of the neighborhood had voted for Andrew Cuomo, a staunch supporter of Israel who campaigned on a tough-on-crime agenda, by a 24-point margin. The more-than-300 comments responding to that anonymous post are full of mothers looking for property in New Jersey or Florida, predicting that Mamdani’s promise to make buses free will lead criminals to rape and kill innocent passengers, and airing their worries that New York City is on its way to becoming 1930s Germany.

A vocal minority of the group’s members jumped in to debate these reactions and point out the Islamaphobic subtext of the anti-Mamdani mania which only led to further fighting in the comments. As more combative threads cropped up over the next 24 hours, some users pleaded for each other to “get a collective grip.” Others posted that they were quitting the group they’d come to for swapping advice on strollers and nannies. “Not fleeing the city,” one wrote. “Fleeing this group. Bye MUES.”

35,000 members. “With all my love for
NYC I can’t believe 50% +- of the city
voted for this joker. Wondering who's
actually leaving? To where, Florida?”

[Slide 3] The more-than-300 comments
responding to that anonymous post
are full of mothers looking for
property in New Jersey or Florida,
predicting that Mamdani’s promise
to make buses free will lead criminals
to kill innocent passengers, and
airing their worries that New York
City is on its way to becoming
1930s Germany.

[Slide 4] A vocal minority of the group’s members
jumped in to debate these reactions and
point out the Islamaphobic subtext of the
anti-Mamdani mania —“It IS racist to just
be mad that your new mayor is a Muslim”

— which only led to further fighting in the
comments. As more combative threads
cropped up over the next 24 hours, some
users pleaded for each other to “get a collective
grip.” Others posted that they were quitting
the group they’d come to for swapping
advice on strollers and nannies. “Not
fleeing the city,” one wrote. “Fleeing

this group. Bye MUES.”

[Slide 5] Robin Reiter, a single mother with

a 13-year-old son, didn’t hesitate to jump
into the mix in response to a commenter
who told angry members to “get your
panties out of a crunch and just relax.”
“We are literally terrified that a mayor
who won’t condemn Hamas and won't
condemn the phrase ‘Globalize the Intifada’
is now running the city with the second
largest Jewish population in the world,”
the 49-year-old wrote. (In July, Mamdani
said he will not use that phrase, and

he has called the October 7 attacks

a “horrific war crime.”)

[Slide 6] Reiter says she’s now considering a move
to Hoboken, New Jersey, as a result

of Mamdani’s win. “It feels very immoral
to me at this moment to pay tax dollars
toa city that just elected someone who
would love to see my people murdered,”
she said. “We're all looking for an out,
because I can’t jeopardize the safety of my
son.” She’s not the only one looking to flee:
There are 360 comments ona post titled,
“Where to now?” where members shared
real-estate-agent contacts and bragged
about their second homes in red states.

[Slide 7] April, who says she is one of a few Black
moms in the Facebook group, scoffed

at those members of the group talking about
fleeing New York City. “No, you're not,” she
says. “Just relax.” The fiery debates don’t
make her want to leave the group either.

She finds any comparison between
Mamdani’s New York and Auschwitz

to be ridiculous, and she especially hates
when members of the group who voted
for Donald Trump say that Mamdani

is not qualified to run the city. She vented
this frustration on a thread where moms
debated the baseless accusation that the
mayor-elect plans to implement Sharia law.

[Slide 8] At the link in our bio,
read the full report on
the Facebook meltdown
over Mamdani.

caption:
Cacio e pepe is harder to make than it seems. If the temperatures and ratios of ingredients aren’t right, the pasta can enter the dreaded “Mozzarella Phase.”

But a group of researchers tested hundreds of different conditions, measured the clumpiness of each sauce, mapped out the results and found a foolproof, award-winning scientific recipe for cacio e pepe. 

Cacio e pepe for two (science edition)
Ingredients:
300g Pasta (tonnarelli preferred)
200g of Pecorino Romano
5g of Corn starch

Recipe: 
1. Cook pasta, saving some extra starchy pasta water just in case.

2. Add corn starch to 50g of water in a small sauce pan, heating and stirring until it becomes gelatinized and thick.

3. Take cornstarch slurry off heat and add 100g of cold water.

4. Mix cheese in, then blend sauce. If too thick to blend, add pasta water.

5. Pour sauce over pasta and garnish with black pepper.

🎤✏️🎞️🎥 Tom Lum / @tomlumperson

The parody of the nobel prizes? In physics! Kachoe pepe is a deceptively difficult dish. After all, it's just three ingredients. Pasta, cheese, and pepper. How hard could it be? But it's combining those ingredients that's made folks like Minji with Babish almost give up on it, calling it easily one of the hardest things I've made. And that's because when the starch from the pasta combines with the protein from the cheese and the heat from the pan, it can easily enter what the researchers call the dreaded mozzarella phase, where the sauce becomes a clumpy, goopy mess. But the specific ratios and temperatures causing this failure point are still a mystery. What are you gonna do? Make hundreds of batches of pasta meticulously controlling each individual variable? How many times did you guys have to make? 450, yes. Now of course these were petri dishes, not full plates, which then let the researchers analyze and measure the clumpiness of the sauce. Which resulted in this beautiful diagram. On the y-axis, we have temperature and that dark red zone is the mozzarella phase. And on the x-axis, we have the ratio of cheese. But what's weird is it doesn't form a straight line. It makes this little u-shape. And that's because cheese actually has two proteins in it, k-scene and whey. And the different proteins denature and interact at different rates, creating this curve and this clumpy danger zone. Now this may seem like a lot of effort for pasta science, but studying how proteins interact and change phase could actually help us answer one of the biggest questions in science. A foolproof scientific recipe for cacio e pepe. Because it turns out if you increase the starch level enough, you can make a sauce that almost never enters that danger zone. And the secret to getting that level of starchiness? Corn starch. media_description: This video is an educational talk where a young man provides advice on how to communicate effectively with a colorist. He explains that the best way for a colorist to understand a client's vision is to use visual references. He suggests that these references can show the colorist what a client likes and dislikes, and he recommends using stock photo websites or social media platforms like Instagram to find examples from various professionals. The speaker then outlines the four basic building blocks of a color grade: contrast, saturation, texture, and color palette. He explains that by thinking about these four categories, a client can better understand what their eye is looking for and communicate their needs more effectively. He uses the metaphors of a therapist and a mechanic to illustrate that having self-awareness and using these building blocks can make the communication process less intimidating. The video is a direct-to-camera monologue with text overlays that reinforce the key points being discussed.
transcript: Here's how I talk about color and some helpful ways to communicate your ideas to a colorist. As a colorist, the easiest way for me to understand the direction that you wanna take a project in is to have visual references. Visual references can also show me what it is that you like about these references versus things that you aren't necessarily paying attention to. Like you could be like, I love the color in this or I love the warmth, but I don't really love the contrast of these. And like having multiple references really helps show that. And personally, if I was looking for a reference, I would use shot deck, frame set or go on Instagram, find some, an agency or a post house. There you can find like directors, DPs, colorists. You can see all broad range of work and you can go on the individual accounts and check out even more work. And when talking about what you want, it's tricky. There's a fine line. There's a fine line because there's a sweet spot between too little and too many words when you're trying to communicate your ideas. So here what I would say are the four basic building blocks of a color grade. I would say that it's contrast, saturation, texture and color palette. Color palette being like hues and texture being like grain, sharpness, softness, stuff like that. By thinking about these four categories, you can help you understand what your eye is looking for. Like you may have the thought to yourself, like I want this to have more pop. And that's a very real thought. That's a very real feeling. And by taking that thought and passing it through the four categories, it might be able to help you pinpoint exactly where you think that the color is lacking. It's like having a therapist, right? Like, well, it is our job to ask the right questions, to understand what your needs are. Having your own awareness can really help you feel understood and address your needs quicker. And unfortunately, on the other side of the coin, again, it's tricky because the pressure you feel to know what you're talking about can make things more confusing. It's like going to the mechanic, right? The more technical language that you use, the more you really have to know what you're talking about. So just having visual references on hand really can get you pretty far. And then when you do need to communicate direction or notes with words, thinking about the four categories, the contrast, saturation, texture, and color palette can help make things feel less intimidating.

caption: The Orphan Trains were a social experiment in the United States between 1854 and 1929, during which an estimated 200,000 orphaned, abandoned, or homeless children from crowded Eastern cities—mostly New York—were sent by train to rural areas across the country to be placed with foster families. Organized by charitable institutions like the Children’s Aid Society and the New York Foundling Hospital, the movement aimed to provide these children with better lives through adoption or indentured labor. While many children did find loving homes, others faced exploitation or abuse, sparking debate about child welfare and leading to the rise of the modern foster care system.

media_description: The video is a powerful and introspective piece that explores the nature of art, creativity, and the human spirit. It begins with a young man, Abraham, posing a profound philosophical question about the divine spirit within us. He then introduces the central metaphor of an artist standing before a blank canvas, symbolizing the potential for creation. The speaker elaborates on his belief that there are two types of people: those who see things as they are and those who see things as they could be. The artist, positioned on the line between these two types, is presented as the embodiment of this creative potential. The video then shows the artist creating art, which serves as a literal representation of the speaker's concept of 'externalizing consciousness.' The speaker argues that art is not an escape from reality but a way to submerge in it, to experience it more fully. The video concludes with a message of hope and self-discovery, urging the audience to reconnect with their inner child and to 'spill parts of themselves into everything that I do.' The video is a beautiful and moving meditation on the power of creativity and the importance of self-expression.

author: harlowsmusings
caption:
Trump spent years demonizing immigrants calling them criminals, threatening mass deportations, separating families, and turning immigration policy into a fear-based tool to rile up his base. But here? The mask slips. When deportations threaten the profit margins of his donor class when farms and hotels start to suffer that’s when he suddenly presses pause. Not for compassion. Not for justice. But for capitalism.

Here’s the core issue:
This isn’t a shift in ideology. It’s a revelation of priorities. Immigrants aren’t being recognized as human beings with dignity and rights—they’re being acknowledged only as “necessary labor” to keep the economy running. It’s exploitation disguised as pragmatism.

Let’s break it down:
	•	He doesn’t “need” immigrants. The country does—for its food supply, service industry, and economic stability.
	•	But instead of treating them as essential members of our society, he labels them “illegals” until their labor becomes too valuable to lose.
	•	This isn’t about reform. It’s about controlling lives—turning immigration policy on and off like a faucet based on what’s profitable.

And let’s be clear—pausing deportations to “save hotels” while still criminalizing people for existing here without paperwork is not humane. It’s modern-day indentured servitude.

So after vilifying immigrants, ripping families apart, and making cruelty a cornerstone of his policy… Trump pauses deportations because he needs cheap labor for farms and hotels?

Immigrants aren’t disposable tools to be used when it’s convenient. They are people. Families. Workers who have always built this country. This isn’t mercy it’s exploitation dressed up as strategy. This isn’t leadership. It’s greed.

author: legacy_grip
caption:
To rig a shot like this traditionally you would rig a few points off the neck or body of the guitar to the camera and support the weight of the camera. 

This makes it hard to operate the shot because you need to support the camera and awkwardly maintain the angle as the guitar moves around. Controlling the movement of the guitar is tough in this instance.

For this rig we created an inner ring and an outer ring both built out of speedrail. Almost like a dumb version of a gimbal with no motors. 

The inner ring was free to pivot on the x axis to allow the camera to tilt up and down independent of the rig’s vertical movement. 

This meant that as the rig got higher, the camera would tilt down. If the rig got lower the camera would tilt up. You could raise and lower the rig by holding onto the outer ring without having to worry about whether you were aiming the camera straight down the neck of the guitar - it did it for you.

Ran a pulley from the top of our rig up and over to some counterbalance to make up and down movement effortless.

caption:
Prison rodeos don’t exist anywhere else in the country, but they thrive in Louisiana each April and October at the Louisiana State Penitentiary (or the Angola State Prison as it’s been nicknamed based on the slave plantation it’s built on).

In October, the rodeo brought in nearly half a million dollars a week in October for the state, largely through the labor of inmates who when not participating in the event can make as little as 2 cents an hour working at the prison. 

Over the years, broken bones, concussions, and snapped necks have become routine, often to jeers from the crowd. Several petitions are found across the internet calling for the state to abolish the event, but none have made it to the prison warden or state legislators.

Outside the rodeo arena, dozens more incarcerated people set up booths to sell their handmade artwork, leatherwork, and woodwork. While some are forced to sell their products behind locked and guarded fences, most others sit out in the open, able to share hugs and laughs with their loved ones.

As one incarcerated person told Capital B, it is the only time he can interact with people outside. It brings back a “familiar” feeling, he said, of being “free to exist.”

The annual Angola rodeo offers both a rare glimpse of humanity and a sobering reminder of the racism driving America’s culture.

caption:
Darwinian gastronomy posits that human preference for spices in food is an evolutionary adaptation linked to their antimicrobial properties, which protect against foodborne pathogens. Spices contain compounds that inhibit microbial growth, offering a survival advantage, particularly in hot climates where the risk of food spoilage is higher due to rapid bacterial growth. Over time, natural selection may have favored individuals with a preference for spicy food, as these individuals would have a lower incidence of food poisoning and higher overall fitness, leading to the perpetuation of spice-enjoying genes in human populations.

media_description: The video opens with a bearded man in glasses reacting to a comment that Democrats are pro-capitalism, immediately agreeing and launching into a rant that both major US parties are fundamentally the same because they uphold capitalism. Using a series of analogies—comparing the parties to plastic cups versus glass plates—he argues that material differences don't change the underlying system. He acknowledges he's filming while sick, adding a self-deprecating touch. As he speaks, he introduces visual aids: bar charts comparing 'Blue,' 'Purple,' and 'Red' states on metrics like income after bills, foster care rates, school shootings, maternal mortality, firearm deaths, and violent crime, sarcastically noting that critics 'don't care' about these outcomes. He holds up a copy of the business book 'Good to Great' to criticize the 'good is the enemy of great' mantra as capitalist propaganda, emphasizing he bought it used to avoid supporting the author. The argument deepens with a historical parallel: side-by-side maps of 1860 slave percentages and 2024 prison populations, showing the same Southern states dominate both, suggesting the prison system perpetuates slavery. He then displays congressional vote records for Israel aid bills, pointing out Republicans consistently vote yes while Democrats vote no, but both fund military actions. Throughout, he berates viewers who won't do their own research, shouting 'go fucking look them up yourself.' The tone remains sarcastic and exasperated, punctuated by profanity. The video concludes with him making tea in a branded mug that reads 'Let's keep the dumbfuckery to a minimum today,' sipping it while thanking someone for coasters, then a black screen with a tip request. The overall message is that partisan squabbles mask shared capitalist interests, and viewers should critically examine data rather than accept narratives. The creator's intent is educational activism, using humor and data to mobilize skepticism of electoral politics.

media_description: This image is a comprehensive and highly structured educational tool designed to demonstrate the profound impact of camera lens focal length on portrait photography. It presents a 3x3 grid of nine individual photographs, each featuring the same subject—a woman with fair skin, blue eyes, and blonde hair—posed identically in a consistent outdoor setting. The only variable across the panels is the lens focal length, which is explicitly labeled in white text at the bottom of each image, ranging from 14mm to 135mm. The sequence begins with a 14mm wide-angle lens, which distorts the subject's facial features and creates a vast, distorted background, highlighting the challenges of using a very short focal length for portraits. As the focal length increases through 20mm, 24mm, 28mm, and 35mm, the distortion lessens, and the perspective becomes more natural and balanced. The 50mm lens, often considered a standard for portraits, offers a familiar and flattering view. The sequence concludes with telephoto lenses of 85mm, 100mm, and 135mm, which dramatically compress the background, creating a very shallow depth of field that isolates the subject with a smooth, blurred backdrop. The consistent lighting and the subject's neutral expression across all nine images ensure that the viewer's attention is solely on the optical differences. This composite image functions as a powerful visual lesson, making the abstract concept of lens choice tangible and demonstrating how photographers can manipulate perspective, depth, and subject isolation to achieve different artistic and technical results. The narrative is one of precision and education, aimed at helping photographers make informed decisions about their equipment.

The BBC's sound effect library is now stocked up with over 33,000 samples to download for free.

The extensive archive has been open to the public since 2018 but has since doubled in size and, as users pointed out on X, is completely free for anyone to access.

The library's sound effects and recordings date back to the 1920s, and comprise those made in the broadcaster's dedicated studio for use in specific BBC programmes, and those captured as field recordings out in the world. 

Indexed into categories, the sounds span everything from footsteps and transport to nature and machines. Among the plethora of sounds covered are reindeer grunts, rain, clocks, horses walking in mud, common frog calls and crowds at the 1989 FA Cup Final. And that barely scratches the surface. 

The sounds have been released under a non-commercial use license (a RemArc License) as part of the BBC's RemArc programme, which is “designed to help trigger memories in people with dementia using BBC Archive material as stimulation".
