The main subject, a man with dark hair and a beard, then appears, speaking directly to the camera. He explains that while modern lighting like LEDs is technically superior, there is a unique 'feeling' to traditional tungsten lighting that cinematographers value. He positions Aputure's new 'Indigo' and 'BLAIR' light engines as a solution that combines the best of both worlds. transcript: Any cinematographer or gaffer worth their salt knows. There are two gold standards when it comes to color rendition, and that is sunlight and tungsten. Technically, tungsten is obsolete. HMIs, fluorescence, and of course, LEDs are better in virtually every single way, except for one. Tungsten just has that feeling. That... Je ne sais quoi. It's the same reason why we shoot on film. It feels right. It looks right. Well, Aputure just killed the obsolete with Blair, the new light engine that's inside of the 1200X. Most of these other manufacturers are chasing RGBACL, and Aputure's coming at it a completely different way by, I don't know, just mimicking the physics of actual sunlight. Okay, so this is all of the frequencies inside of sunlight. The visible light that cameras can actually see is only from about here to here, so why on Earth did Aputure add an indigo chip that straddles the point in which we can even see one word? Fluorescence. So many organic and man-made objects fluoresce to different degrees when they're exposed to the ultraviolet light that's inside of the gold standard. Sunlight, tungsten, and even like carbon arc lights. Aputure just cracked the code on what makes gold gold. The 1200X isn't just about adding bi-color or IP65 or the new ProLoc, good low-end dimming, more output, or even the XY mode. It's about a new gold standard for artificial light. Also, this isn't sunlight. This is a CRLS mirror's bluff bounce and, of course, the new 1200X.

media_description: This video presents a social psychology experiment conducted in a classroom setting, designed to demonstrate how learned helplessness is induced in individuals. The experiment begins with students being given anagrams to solve, starting with the relatively simple 'BAT'. As students successfully complete the first task, they raise their hands, indicating their progress. The teacher then introduces the second anagram, 'LEMON', which is also solvable, but the focus shifts to the third anagram, 'CINERAMA', which is presented as impossible despite being the same as the previous tasks. The teacher explains that students on one side of the room were given tasks they could not solve, leading to feelings of helplessness and frustration. This setup creates a controlled environment where the teacher directly observes and explains the psychological phenomenon of learned helplessness, where individuals stop trying after repeated failures, even when the task becomes solvable. The video highlights the emotional responses of students, including feelings of stupidity, confusion, and frustration, as they witness others succeed while they struggle. This narrative underscores the study's purpose: to illustrate how external factors and social comparison can lead to learned helplessness, a concept often used in academic literature to describe the psychological state of giving up after repeated failures. The teacher's calm, authoritative delivery and the students' visible reactions create a compelling educational narrative that effectively communicates the psychological principles at play.

caption:
Lighting breakdown for a bar location daytime interior in The Cafone  Episode 2, directed by Tom Bentey and shot by @nicholaspietroniro on the #Alexa35 and #CookeS4/i primes.

Our main challenge was achieving a soft toplight source that blended with the darker tonalities of a historical hardwood tavern. Our key was a skirted Litemat 4 Plus boomed overhead with a polysilk 4’x4’ to double break the source.

Lighting for comedy and a daytime interior required some ambient room tone to raise our shadow detail. We used an Aputure Nova 300c pushing through half grid to blend the top source with a cooler ambient nearside fill. Finally we had an Aputure B7c playing as a practical wall sconce to help set the levels and color temperature for the scene.

media_description: This image is a powerful example of internet satire that uses the juxtaposition of a serious religious text with a comical, absurdist image to make a political and social commentary. The text, which quotes Jesus from the Gospel of Matthew, presents a clear theological distinction between true and false converts based on their empathy towards the poor, marginalized, and incarcerated. This message is presented with a sense of gravity and importance. The image, however, is a meme featuring a puppet with a blank, unimpressed expression, a character widely recognized in online culture as a symbol of indifference or lack of comprehension. The humor is derived from the stark contrast between the serious, weighty text and the absurd, trivial visual. The creator is not just making a joke; they are making a pointed statement about the perceived hypocrisy of conservative Christians. They are suggesting that the idea of being 'outwardly religious' without genuine empathy is so obvious that even a puppet can see it. The humor is dark and potentially offensive because it targets a specific religious and political group, generalizing their beliefs and actions in a negative light. The meme format is used to create a sense of irony, where the visual undermines the text, and the text, in turn, gives the visual a deeper, more pointed meaning. The audience for this humor is likely to be those who are already skeptical of conservative Christianity or who appreciate internet memes that use irony to make a political point. The image is not just a joke; it is a piece of cultural commentary that uses the power of the internet to spread a specific worldview. The creator's intent is to provoke thought and discussion about religious authenticity and the nature of belief, using humor as a tool to make their point. The overall effect is a blend of seriousness and absurdity, creating a memorable and impactful message that is both humorous and thought-provoking.

author: thatsnotrightpolitics
caption:
The murder rates in 2020 Trump-voting states have exceeded those in Biden-voting states every year since 2000. Republicans have built their party on being the crime-fighting candidates, even as murder rates in red states have outpaced blue states by an average of 23% over the past two decades.

Despite false claims by Donald Trump that crime has increased under President Joe Biden, PolitiFact confirms that in 2022, the violent crime rate neared a 50-year low. 

That’s not all. Preliminary statistics for 2023 indicate the lowest levels of violent crime ever recorded, dropping below previous records in 2014 and 2019. And that’s still not all, because right now it appears that 2024 is still trending down.

Americans are safer now than they have been in decades, and the numbers have only gotten better under Biden. 

There are fewer violent crimes now than there were in 1971 under Richard Nixon, despite a population that has increased by over 100 million people. Today we are experiencing not simply fewer crimes per person, but fewer crimes overall. According to FBI statistics, there were over 5 million fewer violent crimes in the United States last year than in the final full year of Ronald Reagan's “tough on crime” administration.

After peaking in 1991 under George H. W. Bush, violent crime has been slowly declining year over year. There have been a few exceptions: Some categories of violent crime, including murder, were up in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic. Even then, those numbers didn’t come close to the levels seen in the 1980s or 1990s.
media_description: The video opens with black-and-white images of Republican politicians including Ted Cruz, Marjorie Taylor Greene, and Donald Trump over a grid background, with on-screen text stating 'I'm going to show you how Republicans' claim that "crime is a problem exclusive to blue cities and states," is false.' It then shows clips of Republican figures saying 'Democrat run cities' and 'Democrat-controlled cities,' sourced to Forbes Breaking News 2020 and The Hill 2022. The narrator explains that crime data tells a different story, displaying a line graph titled 'Murder rate in red versus blue states 2000–2021' from Third Way's 'The Two-Decade Red State Murder Problem' (2023), showing the red line consistently above the blue line. Text cites CAP data: from 2015–2022, blue-state cities averaged 7.23 per 100,000 versus 11.1 in red-state cities, 53% higher. It concludes with protest images and a New York Times headline 'After Mass Shootings, Republicans Expand Access to Guns,' stating Republicans make it easier for criminals to get guns, want to appear tough on crime but are soft on guns, a choice proving deadly for all. He explains his motivation came from constituent frustration with a system perceived as rigged, recounts conversations with colleagues Brian Baird and Louise Slaughter about trading on knowledge, and cites data that members of Congress outperformed the market by about 6%. He argues the issue is not about agreeing on policy substance but restoring faith that members are not trading for personal gain, calling insider trading by members a disgrace and a breach of public trust. He urges passage of the bill, emphasizing transparency, fair markets, and a higher standard for public servants, and concludes by quoting SEC Chairman Levitt about maintaining investor confidence. author: nowthisimpact
caption: A 'DEI candidate?' How about 'the more qualified candidate?' This pastor weighs in on all Kamala Harris has done to prepare for leading the country
media_description:
This video captures a powerful moment from a Black pastor's sermon defending Vice President Kamala Harris against racially motivated criticism. Standing at a podium in a light gray suit, the pastor opens by questioning the impossible standards Black people must meet to be considered qualified, listing Harris's impressive credentials: top of her class at Howard University, law school graduate, state attorney general, U.S. senator, and Vice President. His voice grows more impassioned as he recounts how a Tennessee representative dismissed her as a 'DEI candidate,' used the outdated term 'colored,' and deliberately mispronounced her name.

With growing intensity, the pastor declares his refusal to tolerate a white man disrespecting a Black woman, framing this as both personal and communal offense. He then pivots to a pointed comparison, asking rhetorically who is more disqualified than Donald Trump, suggesting Republican support for Trump represents their grievances rather than qualifications. The pastor concludes with a resolute declaration of his own support: 'I'm all in!'

The video's power lies in its unapologetic confrontation of racial double standards in American politics. Through the lens of Black church oratory, the pastor transforms a political defense into a moral crusade, connecting Harris's treatment to broader patterns of racial disrespect. His Southern-inflected delivery and rhythmic emphasis create a sermonic cadence that resonates with traditions of Black prophetic speech. The on-screen captions reinforce his key points, making the message accessible for social media consumption while preserving the raw emotion of his live delivery.

It then transitions to a modern-day basketball game, a football player celebrating a touchdown, and a track athlete in a crouched start, all highlighting the physical and mental effort required to succeed. The voiceover, delivered in a deep, resonant tone, speaks directly to the viewer, stating that while the game may change, the most important thing—the drive from within—remains constant. The final scenes show Jayson Tatum and other athletes in moments of intense focus and celebration, culminating in a powerful message that greatness is an internal quality. The overall message is that the brand is for those who possess this 'inner game' and are driven to be the best.

media_description: This video is a news segment by NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben that investigates the prevalence of sexist political merchandise at Trump rallies. The host introduces the topic by discussing a t-shirt she found that reads 'Biden Sucks! Kamala Swallows!' and features a suggestive slogan on the back. She interviews a Trump rally attendee, Miranda Barbee, who purchased the shirt without knowing its full message, and who defends the language as 'just words.' The segment then expands the analysis to show a history of similar demeaning merchandise targeting female politicians like Hillary Clinton, Sarah Palin, and Nancy Pelosi. The host contextualizes this phenomenon by discussing the political concept of 'hostile sexism' and how it relates to the beliefs of some Trump voters. The video concludes by drawing a parallel between the offensive language on the merchandise and the 'locker room talk' defense used by Trump, highlighting a broader partisan gap in attitudes towards gender and vulgarity in American politics. The overall tone is analytical and informative, with moments of dark humor.

media_description: This video is a concise cooking tutorial demonstrating how to prepare crispy fried chicken tenders. It begins with the creator introducing the dish and providing the recipe website. The tutorial then proceeds step-by-step: raw chicken tenders are tenderized with a fork; they are seasoned with a mix of kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and cayenne pepper; they are coated in flour; then dipped in a wet batter made with flour, eggs, water, salt, and pepper; and finally, they are fried in oil at 325°F until golden brown. For an extra layer of crispiness, the creator recommends a second fry at a higher temperature of 375°F. The video concludes with the creator enjoying the finished product. The creator's enthusiastic narration and the satisfying visuals of the cooking process create an informative and appealing viewing experience.
transcript: Now I fry a lot of chicken, but this technique and the batter I made gave these chicken tenders the most beautiful crust I've ever seen. So good. Optional, but remove the tendon on your tenders with a fork, then in a small bowl combine kosher salt, black pepper, garlic and onion powder, paprika and cayenne and mix to combine. Sprinkle that evenly onto your tenders, then mix them well and let them dry grind while we talk dry batter. This ratio of all purpose flour, potato starch and cornstarch for me is the trifecta for frying. Add a tablespoon of baking powder to the mix and season well with the same spices that we season the chicken with to really reinforce all that flavor. Then adding just a few tablespoons of water and mixing it into the batter is key for creating craggly bits and texture on the chicken so whatever you do, don't skip this step. Make a quick wet batter by combining flour, eggs, water and salt and pepper, then mixing to get the consistency slightly looser than pancake batter. Dip those seasoned chicken tenders in the wet batter letting any excess drip off, then add it directly to the dry mix and really pack it in to make sure every spot is covered until it looks just like this with all those craggly bits. Heat your neutral oil to 325 and fry in batches for 4 minutes where they should look like golden brown. Remove and fry the rest, then I like to use a mesh strainer to get rid of any loose batter before I heat the oil to 375 and fry for another 1-2 minutes until they're deep golden brown and crispy. Once they're all fried up, let them cool and enjoy them with your favorite sauce.

author: therecount
caption: RUDY DOWN
media_description: This 60-second montage captures the essence of the Republican National Convention's second night through a series of tightly edited, emotionally charged soundbites. Opening with the Speaker of the House declaring rights come from God, the video immediately establishes a religious, anti-government-overreach frame. It then pivots to culture war issues, with Sarah Huckabee Sanders mocking the administration's inability to define 'woman' and another speaker calling border security concerns 'racist.' The tone lightens with Nikki Haley's endorsement of Trump, signaling party unity, followed by a bizarre but memorable cut to a West Virginia governor's bulldog 'predicting' Republicans will keep the House. The middle section features blunt policy slogans ('cops are good'), a patriotic 'USA' chant, and a personal story about parents in the federal prison system, broadening the party's appeal. The climax references the recent assassination attempt on Trump as divine intervention, then attacks DEI as 'division, exclusion, and indoctrination.' A musical interlude chanting 'Trump, Trump, baby' and closing jokes about menopause and persecution ('they're after us') end the video on a mix of entertainment and paranoia. Throughout, the visuals—speakers at podiums, the convention hall, the bulldog—reinforce the audio's partisan message, creating a cohesive piece of political persuasion that balances outrage with humor to keep viewers engaged. The creator's intent is clear: to distill hours of convention coverage into a viral, shareable clip that energizes the base and defines the narrative for undecided voters, using emotional appeals (pride, fear, humor) to make the Republican platform memorable and palatable.

author: dr.noc
caption:
😳Where do our opinions come from?🧐

In this series of studies, subjects were asked how they felt about generous and strict welfare programs. As expected, people who were more liberal tended to prefer the generous welfare support programs, and people who were more conservative tended to prefer the more strict programs.

However, when the researchers told the participants fake political poll results, the subjects’ opinions started to mirror the “positions” of their party. For example, if liberal participants were told that 95% of congressional liberals and only 10% of conservatives supported the strict welfare program, they rated it much more favorably.

The scary part is that participants mostly denied having been influenced by knowing the stated “position” of their party. The data told a very different story! This means that this type of “in-group” thinking could easily be affecting you and me without us being fully consciously aware that it is going on.

As always, the full research report contains much more nuance and interesting insights than I can include in a short video, and I encourage you to read it! It was called Party Over Policy: The Dominating Impact of Group Influence on Political Beliefs

#science #psychology #todayilearned #til #drnoc
media_description: The video is a short-form educational piece where a narrator, Griffin Conaboy, explains a psychological study titled 'Party Over Policy'. The study reveals that people's opinions on social welfare policies are heavily influenced by their political party's stance, even when the policy contradicts their initial beliefs. The narrator presents the study's methodology, results, and the most concerning finding: participants denied being influenced by their party's position, suggesting this influence happens at a subconscious level. The video concludes by challenging the audience to consider whether their own beliefs are truly independent.

transcript:
[Slide 1] دينا أول مرة أخذتك عدير حنّة شايفة؟ هاي إنتي بسغيري مع ستو أم علي وهي أنا وهي أمي ويش رسم لكي ديكو
[Slide 2] I'm Lina Suellem, I'm a filmmaker. I was born in Paris from an Algerian father and Palestinian mother. I've been very inspired by family stories, archival footage, because my father was filming a lot in the 90s, so I have a visual heritage. I see a lot of faces and places that today don't exist anymore, and so it's a way to keep on making art through things that already exist. I didn't live exile, but I inherited from this feeling and sensation. I'm really inspired by Edward Said and how he sees exile because I feel the same way and the sense that it's the greatest tragedy that a human being can face, and at the same time, it's a way to reinvent yourself. So you have to create a place for yourself so that you can keep on navigating the world. Through cinema and art, it's also a way to reinvent yourself, reinvent language, and create new imaginary territories in which we can find our place.
[Slide 3] هناك البحر هناك لبنان هناك سوريا وهناك الأردن وإحنا هي أنا بالنص
[Slide 4] And so Bye Bye Tiberias was really a continuation of their Algeria in the sense that I kept on exploring stories of exile and transmission and context of displacement, colonization and through family stories and intimate paths.
[Slide 5] I was easier to film my aunts rather than my mother. It was harder to film my mother, although she is the actress and she's the one who's used to cameras, but she had never been in front of a documentary camera, especially with her daughter behind us, the director. So it has been difficult for us to find our balance and for me to be able to address to my mother, not as her daughter, but as a director. So it took us quite some time to find our balance, but we finally found it. And we both really wanted to be able to find it so that we could tell the story together.
[Slide 6] Ma mère m'a transmis sa langue à moitié. Elle m'a transmis un bout de langue. Quand j'étais petite, elle m'emmenait passer tous les étés dans son village palestinien, Dalhanna. Ce village, elle l'a quitté il y a plus de 30 ans pour réaliser son rêve de devenir comédienne.
[Slide 7] Well, for now I have done two films, so I'm still like young in the practice, but I think the archival footage is essential. It's images that I start with, that I question, that I transform. So it's really a visual element that I have since the beginning. I think writing is essential. I always include in the film some dialogues and voiceover that come from my writing and my thinking and my questioning. And collaborating with artistic collaborators. So it's important for me to have these people around me that allow me to have distance when I work, especially in personal subjects, but also know the language, the culture, and I don't have to explain.
[Slide 8] À chaque fois que je la questionne sur son histoire, elle me répète. N'ouvre pas les douleurs du passé. Je me demande souvent ce que tu serais devenue si t'étais restée. Qu'est-ce que j'en sais, Alina ? Parce que je suis partie.
[Slide 9] And when you film places like Palestine, you also know that there's always a risk of disappearing in Eurasia because it has happened and it's been transmitted to you that this risk is always present and we see that it's happening. So you feel that you also have a responsibility to capture something because you don't know what's going to be left of it. So you feel that while filming, you're also immortalizing a presence that risks of disappearing as well. Either if you film older people and older generation, you're capturing a memory that will stay immortalized. While you capture it and you cherish it, you have this fear of losing it. I have the need to capture and as if my father at the time also had the need to capture. So also he kind of transmitted to me without wanting this need to keep trace of our existence.
[Slide 10] I think you have to follow your instincts because, you know, before making a first piece of art or a first film, you're not an artist yet, but you're already an artist. So you have to believe what you feel is the right thing to do, even if you can make mistakes. But if you don't believe and you follow what people tell you to do, because this is how it has to be, then you don't actually find your voice. And this is the hardest thing to follow your instinct, because when you start and you're not experienced, you tend to want to follow all the advices that are given to you. And of course, some of them are good, but at the same time, you have to find your own voice and sensitivity and subjectivity, and you have to claim it. But I believe the role of an artist is always to question the system and to be political, because being political is also in the way that you create the people that you decide to create with. And I think, yeah, it's the time for artists to speak up. So, you know.

media_description: The video begins with a man in a blue shirt and black shorts, standing in a room with a large dog. He is holding a package of dog treats and is teaching the dog to move a dog bed with its nose. The dog is watching the man and the bed. The man then gives the dog the treats as a reward for moving the bed. The man then places the treats on top of a white dresser. The dog sees the treats and runs to get them. The cat on the cat tree watches the dog. The dog gets the treats and runs away with them. The on-screen text 'Teaching my dog to move objects thinking nothing could go wrong...' and the subsequent text overlays like '*Idea*' and 'NOT sharing!' add a layer of humor to the video. The audio features a man giving calm, instructional commands to the dog, followed by a dramatic, orchestral music piece that creates a sense of tension and urgency. The music is not related to the visual content of the video, which is a common technique to make a mundane event seem more significant and to retain viewer attention. The overall tone of the video is humorous, created by the contrast between the simple, everyday event in the video and the dramatic, over-the-top audio.

media_description: The video is a step-by-step guide to making a 'cheese stuffed butter chicken mac and cheese naan pizza' from a restaurant called Mumbai Dreams. The process starts with a person in a professional kitchen taking a ball of naan dough, adding a filling of shredded mixed cheese, and folding the dough over. The filled dough is then rolled out into a flat, circular shape. In a separate pan, macaroni is added to a butter chicken sauce and mixed together. The rolled-out naan is placed on a tray, and the butter chicken macaroni mixture is spooned onto it. The pizza is then topped with more shredded cheese, cilantro, and a final layer of butter sauce. The finished pizza is placed in an oven to bake. After baking, the pizza is removed, brushed with butter, and sliced. The final shot shows a man taking a bite of the pizza, with the stringy cheese stretching, and then giving a thumbs up, indicating his approval. The video is a clear and detailed presentation of a unique and indulgent food item, from its creation to its final, delicious result.

media_description: This video is an analytical explainer created by a content creator to respond to a viewer's comment requesting an analysis of the 'Skibidi Toilet' meme. The creator, a man wearing glasses and a green t-shirt, stands in front of a brick wall and delivers a structured monologue. He begins by establishing that the word 'skibidi' is interesting because it lacks a formal definition yet can be used adjectivally. He then introduces the linguistic concept of 'pseudowords', citing examples like 'Jabberwock' from Lewis Carroll's poem and gibberish from Dr. Seuss books. He contrasts these intentionally created words with 'skibidi', explaining that its origin is not intentional but rather stems from a random video of a Bulgarian man scat-singing. To illustrate his point, he draws a parallel between 'skibidi' and 'Scooby-Doo', noting that both were inspired by random vocal sounds but were applied to different fictional entities. The creator's intent is to educate his audience about the linguistic classification of this viral internet phenomenon. The tone is informative and analytical, treating the meme with academic seriousness, which creates a comedic effect through juxtaposition.

author: de_con
caption:
I'm no Dolly grip but I definitely like this dolly 😍
Things I didn't mention in the video: 
-you can actually own this dolly instead of lease it 
-they start at $100,000 🤑
-The boom arm is removable to make easier for lifting up stairs in pieces 
 @pantherfilmequipment
@camadeusfilm
transcript: Why don't we have this dolly in the U.S.? This is the Panther S type. It's Panther's direct answer to a Fisher 10 or maybe a Hustler style dolly. It does everything that you'd expect those other ones to do, such as rear steer, crab, roundy around. You also have all the sideboards and accessories that you would expect. It actually fits on any standard track that you'll find in rental houses around the U.S. And just like the Pee Wee, it can actually flip both ways on the track, which I think is super handy. The simulators end with the boom. It is 100% electric unlike the hydraulic counterparts of Fisher and Chapman. And it gives it some really interesting superpowers. Instead of controlling the boom with a valve like on hydraulic dollies, you actually have this almost a zoom rocker on this control. And it also pops off the dolly. So if you want to hand this to somebody else, you can. It's also wireless. So you can either have an wired or wireless configuration. The boom actually can also extend underneath the carriage, which is amazing. And I don't really know when I would use that, but it's cool. You don't have to wait on bumping the dolly. You literally just pop out a battery and pop in a new one. It has this full battery charging system, which is super, super clever. But I think the most compelling part of this being a digital boom is the fact that you can set in and out marks, and it will always hit those marks. You can even bake in a feather to start and slowly easily stop your move. Mind blown. All right, if you're a professional dolly group, please let me know in the comments. Like, if your local rental house had these, would you rent this over a Fisher or a Chapman? I have to know.

media_description: This video is a fast-paced and enthusiastic cooking tutorial for a dish the creator calls 'quesadilla nachos'. The creator, a man in a blue t-shirt, presents the final dish with great excitement, describing each chip as a 'mini quesadilla'. The video then breaks down the recipe into several steps. First, it shows how to prepare the chicken by braising it with spices like chipotle in adobo, cumin, and smoked paprika. Next, it demonstrates how to make the accompanying guacamole with avocado, tomatoes, and cilantro. The recipe then moves on to making the cheese sauce with sharp cheddar, corn starch, and evaporated milk. The most unique step is making the nacho chips themselves by creating small quesadillas with Oaxaca cheese and tortillas, then cutting them into chip-sized pieces and frying them. The video concludes by showing how to assemble the final dish by layering the fried quesadilla chips, cheese sauce, shredded chicken, pickled jalapenos, red onions, guacamole, and cilantro. The creator's energetic and humorous commentary throughout the video frames it as a fun and creative cooking challenge rather than just a simple recipe.
transcript: These are by far the best nachos I've ever made. Each chip is a mini quesadilla. Holy shit, this is good. First, we're gonna braise some chicken. So I got some breasts, green chilies, chipotle and adobo, cumin, garlic powder, smoked paprika, a little bit of oregano, cayenne, orange zest, lime zest, orange juice, lime juice, and some chicken stock. Pressure cook that for 25 minutes, then shred it up. Then some quick pickle jalapenos and red onions, got vinegar and sugar, mix that together. Then for some guac, avocado, tomatoes, pepper, lime juice, onion powder, cilantro, and mix that up. For the star of the show, I got some corn tortillas, Oaxaca cheese, make a little quesadilla, then cut them up into nacho chip sizes and fry them for about a minute and a half. For the nacho cheese, we got sharp cheddar, corn starch, cayenne, cumin, some evaporated milk. That gets mixed up until everything is melted. Now here's the deal. 🪜THE LADDER🪜

Cinematography by @tobyromerodp 
Directed by @emiliofilms 

“The goal was to shoot anamorphic only during our flashback sequences, to elevate our world visually beyond the spherical look we already established. The film follows an aging fisherman in a small Alaskan town with a science fiction twist. So it was important for us to play into that visually. Thanks to Atlas, we were able to come in and test some really funky and experimental anamorphic projects they’ve been pioneering, opting for a mixed bag of various coated Orions along with some other 2x project they’re cooking up. What made these lenses special is that they exaggerate beyond the standard anamorphic look we’re accustomed to. We wanted something that stood out to the viewer, disorienting them with a false sense of reality, much like what our character is feeling in those moments. I think these optics served the story quite well with their unique flaring, extreme distortions, and satisfying sharpness fall-off from center. This is why we were so happy to work with Atlas, they always manage to take an already fantastic anamorphic lens and somehow make it better.” - @tobyromerodp

media_description: This video is a detailed tutorial on how to create a specific lighting effect for photography. The creator, a young man with dark hair and glasses, begins by showing the final, beautifully lit scene of a man sitting in a room with warm, atmospheric lighting that simulates a bright sunny day. He then transitions to a behind-the-scenes view of the same room to explain the process. He describes using a white bounce card from a 5-in-1 reflector to simulate sunlight coming through a window. To enhance the effect, he sets up a Nanlite Forza 300B light at 2700 Kelvin pointed directly at the bounce card to cover the entire window area with soft, natural-looking light. Next, he explains how he adds a 'backlight' using a Nanlite Forza 60C light at 2700 Kelvin positioned above the bounce card and pointed straight down into the room to create the illusion of sun rays leaking in. To further emphasize that it's bright outside, he demonstrates using a Nanlite Forza 60B light at 2700 Kelvin aimed directly through holes in the wall to create subtle light rays. Moving inside the room, he adds ambiance by turning on a lamp with an LED bulb and uses a Nanlite PavoSlim 60C light as a subtle fill light that matches the warmth of the lamp. Finally, he completes the lighting setup by placing a Nanlite PavoTube at 5600 Kelvin into the ceiling fixture as a top light. To pull all the elements together and enhance the atmospheric mood, he uses a haze machine to fill the room with smoke. The video concludes by showing the final shot once again, emphasizing how these techniques combine to create the desired 'moody trap room' aesthetic.
transcript: This is how I made this shot. First, we're going to simulate a bright sunny day. So I'll use this white bounce from a 5-in-1 reflector and bring in the Nanlite Fortza 300B set to 2700 Kelvin pointing directly at the bounce card. This will cover the space of the window, making the light coming in from outside softer and more natural. Now to sell the effect of sunlight even more, I'll place this Nanlite Fortza 60C at 2700 Kelvin right above my bounce card, pointing straight down into the room. This acts as sun rays leaking in and essentially being my backlight. Window number two needs some light to peek through, further showing that it's bright out. So we'll take a Nanlite Fortza 60B at 2700 Kelvin pointed directly through these holes in the wall to get our subtle light rays. Moving inside, I'll turn on this lamp, which just has a LED bulb in it for some ambience. Next, I'll throw in this Nanlite Pavel Slim 60C as a very subtle fill light matching the lamp. Lastly, I'll place this Nanlite Pavel tube at 5600 Kelvin into the ceiling lighting fixture as a top light. To pull it all together, spray some haze in the room, and that's how I got this moody trap room.

caption:
Checking neutrality on @bbcnews. 

Their coverage has consistently shown a disproportionate bias towards Israeli deaths rather than Palestinian ones. These lines in the top chart are largely unaffected by the mounting Palestinian death toll shown in the bottom chart. 

If you look close at that bottom chart, you’ll see that the cumulative Israeli deaths declined on November 10. That’s because Israeli officials revised down their estimate of victims from 1,400 to 1,200. On December 15, the estimate was revised down again to 695 civilians and 373 members of security forces. 

This analysis is based on the majority of published BBC articles relating to Palestine/Israel, scraped between 10/7 and 12/2 by Jan Lietava (@yan.json) and Dana Najjar (@jarz_d), including 672 articles and 4,404 posts in livefeeds. 1,485 documents were automatically tagged as containing sentences relating to death, which were then individually read and manually tagged, based on whether they talked about Palestinians, Israelis, both or neither.

The y-axis is scaled from 20 to 100, and the x-axis displays dates at weekly intervals. The bottom graph is an area chart showing the cumulative number of deaths, with a purple area indicating the cumulative count of Palestinian deaths and a light blue area for Israeli deaths. The cumulative count rises steadily over time, with the purple area growing more rapidly than the light blue area. The visual style is simple and accessible, using a beige background and clear, handwritten labels. media_description: Video essay on the cinematography of La Bola Negra, arguing the secret is blocking: how characters are positioned and moved within the frame.
transcript: La Bola Negra is easily in the running for the best cinematography of the year, and I think the secret comes down to one filmmaking concept, blocking. Blocking is essentially how filmmakers choose to position and move their characters within the frame. And in La Bola Negra, cinematographer Chris Giordano is incredibly precise with it, while somehow making every composition feel completely natural. And I love this because it pushes against a trend that we see in modern filmmaking, where it feels like every shot needs an insanely shallow depth of field and the blurrious background possible. And while that looks certainly has its place, those close-ups can also strip away so much context and limit how much information you can communicate within a single frame. La Bola Negra does the opposite. You'll have multiple characters existing within the same composition, and yet the frame never feels messy. It feels intentional. Your eye always knows where to go, but you're still able to take in the world around these characters. And then you add the fact that it was shot on 35mm, giving every one of these compositions that incredible texture, and you get, without a doubt, one of the best-looking films of the year.

caption: Slice and dice your meat, then grab salt, an oil, a liquid, and a sweetener (optional, but highly recommended). And voila! You've got the perfect marinade.
media_description: America's Test Kitchen cook explains that marinades mostly only flavor the surface of meat: she soaks chicken breasts in different marinades for 18 hours and compares; the caption gives a simple formula of salt, oil, a liquid and an optional sweetener.
transcript: Everything you know about marinades is wrong. Most people think that letting your meat steep in a flavorful mixture with wine, honey, garlic, spices, or citrus allows those flavors to soak in and thoroughly season it, but that's not exactly true. I soak these chicken breasts in a bunch of different flavorful marinades for 18 hours, then cook them, and here's the thing. On their surfaces, they taste great and really different from one another, but when I trimmed off the outer 3mm or so and then tasted the chicken again, I could no longer identify any differences among the samples. Here's why. Most flavor compounds can't actually travel very deeply into meat. The fat-soluble ones are repelled by the water meat contains, and the water-soluble ones that can penetrate are too large to travel more than a few millimeters. The big exception is salt. With time, salt can migrate deep into the meat to enhance its flavor and alter its protein structure, so it cooks up tender and juicy. To use this information to your advantage, start by maximizing your meat's surface area by slicing, pounding, or cubing your meat before marinating. Then make sure to include salt or salty ingredients like soy sauce in your marinade and give the salt plenty of time to do its magic. Finally, make sure to include an oil in addition to a liquid in your marinade. That way, both the fat and water-soluble flavors get dispersed throughout the liquid and onto the food. Bonus points. Add a sweetener like sugar, honey, or molasses to ensure your marinated meat browns well and develops a nice crust.

caption:
The muscle nobody trains, and how to actually train it 👇

Your lower trap pulls your shoulder blade down and helps rotate it so your arm can go overhead cleanly. The problem is your upper trap is stronger and always ready to take over, so the cue matters far more than the weight.

Prone Y raise. Lie face down on an incline bench, arms in a Y above your head, thumbs pointing up. Lift your arms toward the ceiling without letting your shoulders creep toward your ears. Start with no weight at all. If you feel it at the top of your shoulders or your neck, your upper trap has taken over, so go lighter or smaller.

Wall slide. Forearms on the wall, slide them up overhead. At the top, keep your arms up and pull your shoulder blades down your back. That combination of arms up and blades down is exactly the job your lower trap does, and it’s usually the part people can’t do at first.

Rows with the shoulder set first. Before every row or pulldown, pull your shoulder down away from your ear, then pull. Most of us shrug through every rep, which just trains the upper trap again.

Overhead carry. Hold a light weight straight overhead and walk slowly. Keep your ribs down and don’t let your lower back arch. This teaches the lower trap to hold your shoulder blade in position under load.

10–15 slow reps, 2–3 times a week, stopping before failure. It’s a thin, flat muscle, so it won’t make you bulky.

What it won’t change: your bones. The width of your shoulders is set by your collarbones, and the depth of your upper body by your ribcage. Neither can be trained. It also won’t shrink an upper trap that’s already well developed, because you can’t un-build muscle, only stop overloading it.

What it can change is position: shoulders sitting down instead of hiked up, a longer neck line, and ribs that stay down when your arms go overhead. Same frame, held differently. Not smaller. Longer.

And everyone trains this usually by accident. And this is one that actually makes your neck look shorter when it's overdeveloped. But this is only actually the top third of the muscle. It actually runs all the way down your back to the middle of your spine. And the lower portion of the muscle does a completely opposite job. So the top pulls your shoulder up towards your ear. The bottom part pulls it down and away from it. So one muscle has two opposing halves. And basically everyone has an overdeveloped top and an underdeveloped bottom. And that's why your shoulders look rounded and forward when you're trying to pull your shoulders back and down. Today we're talking about the lower trapezius. Now there is a reason you've never trained it. It's basically invisible. She sits flat against your mid back. Doesn't show in a mirror and it's not specifically written on any gym plan. She's one of the only muscles that doesn't have an exercise named after her. Meanwhile, the upper trap gets trained constantly. Every shrug, every heavy carry, every time you lift anything when you're slightly stressed. And this muscle actually tenses when you're anxious. So one half is being hammered daily and the other half has been untouched for years. And the result is this, looking compressed and short through the front rather than opening up your whole middle line. So here's how this actually works. The trapezius is one sheet of muscle shaped like a diamond. It runs from the base of your skull across both shoulders and down to the middle of your spine. It is huge and the fibers run in all different directions. At the top, they run downwards and outwards from your neck. When they contract, they pull your shoulder blade up. In the middle, they run horizontally. So they pull towards your spine. And at the bottom, they run upward and outward from your mid spine. So when they contract, they pull your shoulder blade down. So that's one muscle running in three different directions. Now for your arm to go fully overhead, your shoulder blade has to rotate upwards. And your lower trap is one of the main drivers of that rotation. So when it isn't working, your arm can't go overhead cleanly. Your body compensates the only way that it can. It shrugs or it arches your ribs, which is why so many women's ribs flare when they reach their arms up. And rib flare closes that gap between your ribs and your hips. And that's where your waist lives. So a dormant muscle in your mid back is affecting your neckline. It's affecting your shoulder position and your waist. So why haven't you trained it before? And that's because it only works when your shoulder blade moves downward. And almost nothing that you do in your daily life demands that movement. When you're in the gym, rows pull inward. But a lot of people shrug through this movement, so it's activating the upper trap instead of the lower. And it's a weak muscle with a bad mechanical position. So if the upper trap is strong and willing, it will take all of that brunt. And that's actually the problem here. It's not only under-trained. It's actively being overridden by the stronger half every time that you move. So how do you actually train it? First one, do prone wire raises. Second one, wall slide with a reach. Three, every time you do a row, have your shoulders down first. So before you pull, actively depress your shoulder blades from your ear. And then on this overhead carries with your ribs down. → Only the final answer comes back to the model

transcript: There's a new shift happening in the AI industry. Companies are moving away from the traditional MCPs and picking a completely different architecture instead. Let's break it down in 30 seconds. So we all know the drill. If an AI agent wants to use a tool, you use an MCP. MCP is the standard. It's how an AI agent discovers the tools and calls them. But this technique has a fundamental problem. You would think that everything is smooth, but it's not. For example, my agent needs to find a customer. That's one tool call. Then it has to fetch the customer's order. That's the second tool call. Every single result goes back to the model before the next step starts. And every tool's definition sits inside the model's context throughout the whole time. Now scale that to thousands of tools. Cloudflare hit this exact wall so they build something they call code mode. Instead of handing the model a big list of tools, they convert the tools into TypeScript API. The model now sees just one tool, which is RunCode. It writes a small script and that script runs inside a locked sandbox. The in-between data never comes inside the model. Only the final answer does. And their reason is models are simply better than writing code than at calling tools directly. Anthropic published the same pattern. One example dropped 150,000 tokens to just 2,000 tokens. I found this architecture completely fascinating. media_description: Treehouse Detective on why sitcom tapings are secretly funny off-screen: warm-up comedians like Mark Sweet (Cheers, Everybody Loves Raymond, Big Bang Theory) keep live audiences laughing for hours between takes, often funnier than the show itself.
transcript: The unfunniest sitcoms you've ever seen are actually secretly hilarious but the jokes are all happening off-screen and the story is fascinating. The real comedy isn't happening on camera or even behind the scenes and it's all because of one technical aspect of production. You see, most multi-camera sitcoms throughout history are shot in front of a live studio audience so that they can create a sense of energy for the actors on camera and also so that they can record a laugh track that can be used in the final episode to help sell the jokes. And it sounds like attending a sitcom taping would actually be a lot of fun but the reality is a little bit different than that. You see, sitcom tapings are grueling three to five hour ordeals where every scene is shot multiple times and you're expected to laugh just as hard at take five as you are at take one even if take one wasn't even that funny to begin with. And so for decades, in order to keep the audience energetic, happy and ready to laugh, sitcoms employ warm-up comedians whose entire job it is to just keep you entertained in between takes so that you'll have the best possible reaction to the actual show. Literally for three to five straight hours every single time the director calls cut the warm-up comedian has to immediately jump up and launch into a fresh bit to make sure that the audience doesn't get listless or bored. And honestly, most of the time the warm-up comedian is significantly funnier than the show itself. And they have to be because they're literally tricking you into thinking that the show was funnier than it actually is by association. After laughing hysterically at the comedian for a few minutes, you're much more willing to laugh at the show itself even if it isn't that funny. And the funniest thing about it is is that it doesn't even actually work. I have a whole other video about the fact that most laugh tracks and sitcoms are actually edited in and post because they can't get the in-studio audience to laugh at the show. So at a lot of these tapings you have the audience laughing their asses off at the warm-up comedians and then just going stone quiet for the show itself. These sitcom audience MCs are usually stand-up comics who never quite broke into the mainstream and then just kind of fell into this as a career. And they have some of the most thankless and difficult jobs in show business. They have to stand in front of this audience ready to jump up at a moment's notice when the director calls cut and then cut themselves off mid-sentence anytime the production is ready to shoot again. And they have to do this non-stop for hours. I actually recently went to a sitcom taping which is what inspired me to make this video and the warm-up comic for that taping was this guy named Mark Sweet who's a veteran warm-up comics who's been doing it since the 80s. He was the warm-up comic for Cheers. Everybody loves Raymond, Reba, the Big Bang Theory and a bunch more. And this guy is genuinely hilarious. I mean, funnier than a lot of mainstream famous stand-up comedians. Nobody else in the industry has to perform like this and also gets such a fraction of the credit for it. I mean, nobody knows about these people. Mark Sweet has been doing this for decades and there's barely any information about him on the internet other than his own professional website. And yet he's, I'm not joking. He's genuinely one of the funniest stand-up comedians you will ever hear.
